Round 2503.decision_summary:
THE PENDING BUFFER NOW HONOURS THE BOUND THE USER SET, AT BOTH SITES.
`ext-pubsub-advanced-history`'s clause (4) said wz's live gate is
unbounded where upstream spills. Reading upstream sharpened the defect
before any code was written: unbounded is CORRECT when the user set no
bound -- `zenoh-ext/src/advanced_subscriber.rs` @ `let max_history_depth = conf`
reads `.history.as_ref().and_then(|h| h.max_samples).unwrap_or(usize::MAX)`
-- so the defect is not "wz is unbounded", it is that wz IGNORES the
bound the user set. The clause should be read that way.

THREE THINGS THE PLAN GOT WRONG, each found by reading rather than by
building, and each would have shipped as a defect or a false test.
· THE RESIDUAL NAMES ONE SITE AND THERE ARE TWO. wz inserts into
  `pending_samples` in the history arm AND in the forward-gap arm, and
  upstream guards both. A build that trusted the clause would have left
  the gap arm growing without limit.
· THE TWO SITES ARE NOT UNDER THE SAME FEATURE. The history insert is
  `#[cfg(feature = "ext-pubsub-advanced-history")]`; the gap insert sits
  under `if retransmission` and compiles with history OFF. A bound read
  from `HistoryConfig` cannot simply be used there. ⭐ Upstream settles
  what the off case should do: with no history config the bound IS
  `usize::MAX`, i.e. no spill -- so gating the gap spill on the history
  feature is upstream's own answer, not a wz shortcut, and the code says
  so at the site.
· THE ORDER IS INSERT-THEN-SPILL, so the buffer transiently holds
  depth + 1. Copying it matters: check-then-insert would drop the sample
  that just ARRIVED instead of the oldest one.

AND THE SPILL DELIVERS RATHER THAN DROPPING, which is the whole reason
this is `deliver_and_flush` and not a `pop`. A "bounded" buffer that
dropped would satisfy any length assertion and lose a sample in silence.
That is why every assertion in the new cases reads the DELIVERED vector
and none reads the buffer's length.

⭐ THE TESTS ARE PAIRS, and the pairing is what makes them evidence. Each
case feeds identical samples twice, changing only the bound: at the
ceiling the oldest is delivered (and its contiguous successor drained
with it), and at `usize::MAX` nothing leaves early. Without the second
arm "the buffer is bounded" and "the test never filled it" are
indistinguishable -- the population-of-zero shape this tree keeps
meeting.
⚠ AND THE FIRST DRAFT OF THE BOUNDED ARM WAS WRONG IN A WAY THAT WOULD
HAVE PASSED. It asserted the spill fires on the THIRD sample. Tracing
the depth-2 path by hand shows it fires on the SECOND -- insert, insert,
len == 2, spill -- after which `deliver_and_flush` drains the contiguous
successor. The draft's assertion still held at the end of the sequence,
so the test would have gone green while describing a mechanism the code
does not have.

carried the declaration. The register's FIRST MOVE was to derive
whether the links plane's order and the fold's order are the same,
because the mechanism the item names stands on that. They ARE:
`Dissection::message_lists_with_origin` chains the STREAM lists first,

With the premise established the mechanism is this module's own

declaration must not name a reference that came before it. The walk it

capture holding one list the two orders coincide, which is why this
survived; for a SESSION SPANNING TWO LINKS they do not, and a
declaration sent on the second link before a reference on the first is,
in list order alone, in the future.

is not a second pass and not a deferred resolve: it is the SAME single
pass, walked in the order the heading already claims. The rule that
heading protects is untouched — a declaration still cannot name a
reference that preceded it — and what changes is only that "preceded"
is now measured on the capture instead of on the walk.

share a state exactly as they do upstream.

retransmission at an equal instant drops. Strict, not `<=`.

`handle_live` (recovery on) are cfg-split, but this case does not depend on

R2527 LEFT THIS DELIBERATELY AND ITS REASONING WAS HALF RIGHT. It said a
vendored C submodule crossing a MINOR is a different risk from a Rust patch
release, so it should get its own round. Right to hold the round back; wrong
about the size. Applying R2527's own move — measure the most expensive risk
before committing — the public-header delta between the two versions is:

  1. `zp_spin_once`: `void` -> `bool`. ONE changed declaration.
  2. a `z_timestamp_new` doc clarification (timestamps from one session are
     strictly increasing) plus a `Z_TEST_HOOKS`-gated override typedef, which
     is test scaffolding and not consumer ABI.
  3. one doc-comment word in `types.h`.

That is the whole thing. A minor version number is not a size estimate.

AND THE ONE CHANGE WAS A REAL DEFECT, which is why the measurement was worth
taking rather than assuming a patch-shaped diff meant nothing to do. wz's
drop-in exported `zp_spin_once` returning `void`. A caller compiled against
1.10.1's header expects a `bool` back, so the moment the submodule moved, wz's
ABI mirror was wrong at exactly one symbol.

WHAT THE VALUE MEANS, in upstream's words: "Returns `false` if there are no
more tasks that can be executed immediately. This can only happen when
`Z_RUNTIME_IDLE_READ_TASK_SLEEP` is set to positive value; otherwise read
tasks always reschedule immediately, and `true` is always returned unless the
session is closed." Under the default configuration that reduces to "the
session is still alive", and that is what wz answers. wz never returns `false`
for "no work to do" because it has no task queue to be empty — the same
one-directional divergence the shim's existing docs describe, not a new one.

⭐ IT IS ALSO A STRICT IMPROVEMENT ON THE OLD SHIM, and the old doc says so
against itself: it recorded as a limitation that "pico reports no status here,
so a null or dead session cannot be signalled to the caller". Upstream has
since given the call a channel for exactly that, and wz now uses it.

BURIED: NOTHING IN THE TREE GRADES THIS SIGNATURE. Reverting to `void` leaves

leaves the single-threaded drop-in arm passing. So the fix is correct against
the header and is UNGUARDED. That is a finding for a later round, not

because it survived a list.

*** THE ITEM'S OWN REMEDY IS REJECTED, AND THAT IS THE ROUND'S FIRST JUDGEMENT. ***
The item asks that the pin literal become ONE, everything else parsing or
importing it. Opening the sites says the opposite. A constant that spells the
pin is a TRIPWIRE, not a copy: it exists so that moving the pin FORCES a human
to re-derive the paired data the file carries.
`scripts/lib/sn_resolution_words.py:236` states the reason in its own refusal --
"a mapping carried across a pin bump is one nobody re-read". Dissolving those
literals into an auto-read would DESTROY the tripwire, which is the very defect
the item was filed about. The item told the taking round to judge whether
consolidating is worth anything first; the answer is no.

WHAT A TRIPWIRE NEEDS IS THE OTHER HALF -- SOMETHING THAT TRIPS. A constant
whose file never READS a pin SSOT cannot compare, so it never trips; it just
grades quietly against whatever it last said.
`scripts/lib/upstream_feature_census.py:134` was exactly that. Its
`UPSTREAM_VERSION` was compared only against the version of the zenoh SOURCE
TREE it happened to find, never against the pin -- while its comment ASSERTED
the binding its code did not make ("build-zenohd.sh asserts the same equality").
`build-zenohd.sh` does assert it, but only when it RUNS. On a machine whose
checkout was provisioned by hand, the constant and the checkout can be stale
TOGETHER, agree, and report green; only hosted CI, which provisions AT the pin,
ever disagrees. That is the both-operands-stale shape R2535 paid a hosted red
for.

So the round builds the missing half: `scripts/lib/pin_constant_binding_gate.py`
(pre-push gate 2y, run-ci Layer C0), which classifies every occurrence of a

instruction to stop optimising for the smallest increment and do the thing that

it can be held WEAKLY.

*** THE RESIDUAL IS ONE CLAUSE AND IT IS STRUCTURAL, WHICH IS WHY IT SAT. ***
`liveliness-token`'s tail leaves exactly one open clause -- the aggregate clause
was RETRACTED when upstream reorganised its HATs, and `undeclare`-returns-Result
plus Drop-logging were built in earlier rounds. What remains: wz's token holds a
strong `Session` clone where upstream holds a `WeakSession`
(`zenoh/src/api/liveliness.rs` @ `session: WeakSession`), so a live token keeps
its whole session alive. The reason calls that "an ownership change with a
lifetime consequence across the handle family and is not a bolt-on", and
measuring it says the reason was right about WHY: upstream can express a
`WeakSession` because ITS `Session` is `Arc<SessionInner>`, so `Weak` has
something to point at. wz's was a VALUE STRUCT of nine fields whose `clone`
bumped each field's own `Arc` separately -- there was no single `Arc` for a
`Weak` to reference, and no amount of work inside the token could have made one.

FEASIBILITY WAS MEASURED BEFORE ANY EDIT, and it is what made this one round
rather than a rewrite: `Session` has 72 methods and ZERO take `&mut self`. Every
one is `&self`, so an `Arc` needs no interior mutability, and a `Deref` to the
inner keeps all 72 -- and every `self.field` read -- compiling untouched. The
whole surface needed THREE adjustments: two by-value builders and the two
constructors' struct literals. The compiler confirmed it, once: the first check
of the split produced exactly one error.

⛔ NO `DerefMut`, deliberately. Mutation through a shared handle is what the old
value struct made impossible, and a refactor that quietly introduced it would
trade a leak for a data race. The two by-value builders use `Arc::make_mut`,
which forks ONLY when another handle exists -- precisely when the old
`base.clone().with_…()` forked too, a shape the session tests actually use -- so
the semantics callers see are the ones they always saw.

⚠ WHAT THIS ROUND DOES NOT CLAIM: the token still holds a STRONG handle, the
atom is still PARTIAL, and REMAINING WORK is still 59. This is the foundation
the change needs, not the change. Converting the four handles that hold a strong
clone is step 2.

⛔⛔⛔ THE CITATION FORM RULE, learned by shipping it wrong three times: write an
upstream claim as `<root-included path>` @ `<needle>` ON ONE LINE. Three
separate ways to get it wrong, each with its own budget: no needle = BARE, a
line range = LINE-FORM (and adding a root to a line-form citation does NOT
repair it, it just moves it into a budget already at its line), no root =
ROOT-LESS. The scanner is LINE-BASED, so wrapping a path away from its needle
silently converts an anchored citation into a bare one -- that mistake turned
a 6-citation repair into a 6-citation regression inside this round.
⛔⛔ THE RATCHET HAS A PROPERTY WORTH KNOWING BEFORE YOU TRIP IT: a segment
becomes a graded CANDIDATE once the tree demonstrates it is a real upstream
directory, so writing one citation correctly can PROMOTE its segment and make
sibling root-less citations countable -- the residue can go UP when you repair
something. That is not damage; it is the debt beside yours becoming visible,
and the honest move is to pay it rather than to leave your own citation
root-less so the segment stays hidden.

Wire the MCU multicast re-join that R2560 decided but could not perform, and take its shape from the AP twin rather than re-deriving it.

THE ROUND WAS HANDED ITS SUBJECT, WHICH IS THE POINT OF THE PRECEDING ONE. R2560 moved `warrants_rejoin()` beside `MulticastOutcome` and closed by stating what it had NOT done: "nothing re-joins yet. The MCU profile can now ask and the answer is `true`, and that is the whole of it." It then measured THREE constraints off `crates/wz-runtime-tokio/src/multicast_glue.rs` @ `async fn rejoin_group_driver<F, Fut>(` and recorded that taking them from there costs nothing while re-deriving them costs a round. All three were taken, and all three survived contact: (i) the rebind is a CLOSURE rather than an enum of face kinds, (ii) it returns an OPTION whose `None` means the host stopped while the face was down, so the caller reports the ORIGINAL loss rather than a re-join it never made, and (iii) the wait is RACED against the stop rather than serialized after it. R2560 flagged (iii) as the one that does not translate -- the AP races a `watch::Receiver` in `tokio::select!`, the MCU loop has no suspension point and takes its stop as a PREDICATE -- and the answer is the one that round predicted: POLL the predicate across a deadline instead of sleeping through it, which is the idiom this module already uses twice for `next_join_ms` and `next_sweep_ms`.

A FOURTH CONSTRAINT WAS NOT IN THE CARRY AND IS THE ONE THAT DECIDED THE SIGNATURE. The first draft re-used a single dispatcher across joins and FAILED, with the socket genuinely re-bound and the carrier back: the second run returned `MulticastOutcome::Stopped` immediately, because the drive loop's first act is `session_state() != Running` and `notify_link_lost` had already driven the FSM into `Stopped` -- a `<final>` in `sources/session/session_fsm_multicast.scxml` @ `<final id="Stopped">`, which cannot carry an outgoing transition. THAT READING INVITES EXACTLY THE WRONG REPAIR: add a resume edge to the statechart and regenerate. The AP twin had already settled it one crate away -- `crates/wz-runtime-tokio/src/multicast_glue.rs` @ `// A FRESH dispatcher per join -- see the egress twin: the peer table` -- for a reason about the DATA rather than the state machine: the old peer table "describes members reached over the link that just died". So the signature takes a dispatcher FACTORY, a fresh session enters at `Running`, and the statechart is untouched. Do not resume a session that is over; start a new one.

THE DRIVER IS TAKEN BY VALUE AND THE DROP IS EXPLICIT, and this is the one part that is not taste. `vendor/lwip/src/core/udp.c` @ `/* port matches that of PCB in list and REUSEADDR not set -> reject */` returns `ERR_USE` unless every PCB on the port sets `SOF_REUSEADDR`, which this tree never does -- verified as a NEGATIVE claim by derivation rather than assertion: `SOF_REUSEADDR` occurs nowhere in `wz-link-lwip`. So the tempting `&mut driver` plus `*driver = rebind()?` CANNOT WORK, because Rust evaluates the new bind while the old PCB is still installed. Taking the driver by value lets the `drop` precede the re-bind, in that order, visibly. The finite `MEMP_NUM_UDP_PCB` pool gives the same answer a second way: a transient double occupancy is a `PcbExhausted` risk on a device sized for one.

THE DELAY IS CONSTANT, AND THAT IS THE PARITY ANSWER RATHER THAN AN OVERSIGHT. The AP faces grow their backoff because a router holding a group face on a flapping NIC would otherwise retry at 1 Hz for the length of the outage. This profile's parity target is pico, whose multicast lease failure arms the same reopen task its unicast failure does and re-arms FLAT: `vendor/zenoh-pico/src/net/session.c` @ `return _z_fut_fn_result_wake_up_after(1000);`. A constant delay is what the upstream this loop mirrors actually does, so R2560's open question about hoisting `RetryPolicy` into `wz-session-core` is not answered here and did not need to be -- this face does not want the schedule.

R2560'S ERROR-CLASSIFICATION QUESTION IS ANSWERED BY PLACEMENT, and the answer is recorded because the question was asked as a precondition. That round found pico's reopen CLASSIFIES failures -- six error codes re-arm, anything else logs and closes -- while wz's AP side retries on ANY `std::io::Error`, and asked whether the MCU wiring should classify. IT DOES NOT, AND DELIBERATELY: the rebind is a closure the HOST supplies, so the host is where a classification would live, and this loop cannot see an error at all -- it sees `Some`/`None`. The two populations do not correspond in any case, measured rather than assumed: pico's list is about session OPEN, while what fails here is a socket bind whose error vocabulary is `LinkError` -- `PcbExhausted`, `BindFailed(i8)`, `MulticastJoinFailed(i8)` -- a disjoint set. Authenticate the one GitHub REST call this workspace's CI makes, so Layer Qz stops dying on a rate limit it shares with strangers -- and adjudicate, rather than inherit, the uncommitted repair a cancelled run left in the tree.

THIS ROUND INHERITED WORK IT DID NOT WRITE, AND THE FIRST DUTY WAS TO JUDGE IT. A previous run was cancelled mid-round and left `.github/workflows/ci.yml` modified (+53/-3) with no commit. The standing instruction for that state is neither to trust it nor to discard it but to re-derive its premises independently and then finish or refute it. Every premise was re-derived this round from primary sources, and all of them hold; the diff is committed essentially as found, and this entry records the re-derivation rather than the authorship.

THE DEFECT IS AN ANONYMOUS CALL TO A PER-IP BUDGET. `west sdk install` asks the GitHub releases API which SDK to fetch. Until this round it asked with no credentials, and unauthenticated REST calls are rate-limited PER SOURCE IP. A hosted runner's IP is shared with every other customer on that machine, so the budget can already be spent before the job starts. Run 34599628250 is the failure: the API's own 403 names the runner's address and says so in its body, and upstream's `fetch_releases` prints the prescription by name -- "Try executing install script with --personal-access-token argument or use a .netrc file".

THE BASE IS wz-SIDE, WHICH IS WHY THIS ROUND REPAIRED RATHER THAN REGISTERED. The turn's standing rule is that a base upstream of this repository must be registered and handed back, not patched here. This base is not upstream: upstream ALREADY offers the mechanism, documents it, and prescribes it in the very error it raised. What was wrong was a wz build choice -- our workflow declined a credential that Actions mints for free on every run. There is nothing to ask upstream for.

THE POPULATION WAS ASKED STRUCTURALLY RATHER THAN ASSUMED, because repairing the instance is not the same as repairing the class. The class is "a GitHub REST call this workflow makes anonymously". Enumerated over the whole workflow, it has exactly ONE member, and it is the one repaired. The other two GitHub fetches (shellcheck, actionlint) are release-ASSET downloads at pinned versions against a different host and a different budget, so they are not in the class rather than being unfixed members of it. Had the count come back greater than one, fixing only Qz would have been fixing the instance.

THE THREE GREEN Qz RUNS BEFORE THE RED ARE NOT EVIDENCE THAT THE CALL WORKED, and this is the part most likely to be misread later. The provisioning step is guarded by `if: cache-hit != 'true'`, so a warm cache SKIPS it entirely and those runs never made the call at all. The failure is therefore STRUCTURAL while presenting as intermittent -- it surfaces only on a cache miss. The same consequence applies forward: leaving the cache key alone would have let the next warm run return a green that means nothing, because it would not have exercised the repaired path. Moving the key is what turns the next run into a real test, so the bump is the VERIFICATION half of this round rather than housekeeping.

⭐ THE THREE RESIDUALS WERE ONE MISSING STRUCTURE, which is why they closed together rather than one per round. R2566 built the first (the authenticated username reaching session state). The other two -- no `dictionary_file` loader, no runtime `add_user` / `del_user` -- looked like separate capabilities and were not: wz had NO SHARED CREDENTIAL STORE and no config-driven construction path for the auth plane at all. `UsrPwdMethod` OWNED its `(user, password)` table by value, so every session held a private copy and a mutation after construction reached nothing; `initiate_and_open_session_with_auth` receives an already-built `AuthDispatch` from its caller. zenoh's per-handshake FSM instead holds a REFERENCE to a shared store (`io/zenoh-transport/src/unicast/establishment/ext/auth/usrpwd.rs` @ `inner: &'a RwLock<AuthUsrPwd>`), which is exactly why its mutation verbs take effect at all. Build the store and both clauses close at once.

THREE DESIGN DECISIONS WERE CORRECTIONS MADE BEFORE ANY CODE EXISTED, each settled by reading upstream at the pin rather than by compiling and seeing.
(1) THE ACCESSOR LENDS RATHER THAN RETURNS. `password_for(..) -> Option<Vec<u8>>` is the obvious signature once a lock is involved, and it would copy a password into a fresh, un-zeroized heap buffer on every handshake -- strictly WORSE exposure than the borrow it replaced, in an authentication path. Upstream does not: it takes its read lock and passes the BORROWED password straight to `hmac::sign`, owning only the public username. ⚠ This would have compiled, passed every test, and degraded a security property silently -- no gate in this tree grades posture.
(2) IT IS SYNCHRONOUS DELIBERATELY. Upstream's `recv_open_syn` is `async` and takes an async lock, but `AuthMethod::accept_recv_open_syn` is not; following upstream would have forced the entire auth plane async for one lookup. `wz_runtime_core`'s `with_mutex_mut` is already a synchronous SCOPED CALLBACK, so the shape was in the tree.
(3) AN EMPTY TABLE MUST FOLD TO `None`. `lookup.is_empty()` was the sentinel for "not a responder" at four sites; promoting it to `Option` is the improvement, but wrapping an EMPTY table in a source would invert an authentication default -- a node that does not respond to usrpwd becomes one that rejects every peer. Upstream folds identically (`from_config` yields `None`, never an empty table).

THE BASE: a facade feature must reach EVERY runtime that can carry it. The 5.20 atom's surviving residual was that `crates/wz`'s `switchboard` forwarded to `wz-runtime-tokio` ALONE, so `wz --features runtime-coop,switchboard` activated NOTHING and an MCU consumer had to depend on wz-session-core directly to name the ingress port. That is not a missing capability -- the core side has been MCU-ready since R311y824 made the generated value path take `&mut dyn EventInjector` -- it is a hole in the facade, and cargo's optional-dep `?` is what hid it: it yields the EMPTY SET when the named dep is absent instead of erroring, so the facade advertised a capability one profile could not reach and nothing said so. The sibling forwards one screen up in the same manifest (`codec-close`, the keyexpr family) all name BOTH arms, so the line had drifted out of a shape its own neighbours kept.
THE FIX IS TWO-HALVED ON PURPOSE. The feature forward alone answers only the first clause of the residual. The second -- an MCU consumer needing wz-session-core directly -- is answered by a crate-root re-export in wz-runtime-coop, which is the route `scout_static` already takes across the same facade -> runtime -> core edge. Shipping the forward without the re-export would have moved the tag while leaving half the sentence true.
NOT ALLOC-GATED, and the asymmetry is the design: `EventInjector` is unconditional in wz-session-core because the MCU generated static match calls it, so the port lands on the no-heap profile deploy/mcu-noheap-probe builds with no `#[global_allocator]`.

THE BASE IS A SHAPE, NOT FIVE KNOBS, AND THE ORACLE IS WHAT SETTLED IT. This round set out to close `storage-backend-filesystem`, whose single residual reads "wz honours NONE of the five fs-volume backend properties" and prescribes a SEAM round. The seam it names was built by R2571 (`crates/wz-session-core/src/storage_config.rs` @ `pub volume_cfg:`), so the prescription was finally followable -- but the properties' own definitions were not on this machine, and this tree's rule is that upstream is read, never recalled.

Reproducing the correct reading cost one command.
WHAT THE READING REFUTED. Upstream maps a key to a REAL PATH in a user's directory tree, which is what gives `follow_links` and `keep_mime_types` anything to decide -- symlink-aware existence tests and a walk for the first, a mime guess from the file EXTENSION for the second. wz maps every key to `k<hex16(fnv1a64(key))>` in ONE flat directory with its own serialized frame, so there is no extension, no tree and no symlink. Two of the five are not unhonoured knobs; they are consequences of a SHAPE wz does not have. Three (`read_only`, `on_closure`, `dir`) do have use sites.
THE OWNER CHOSE THE WIDER ANSWER: wz's fs backend should MIRROR the user's directory tree, full parity, rather than remain an opaque durable store. That makes the residual a redesign whose first leg is the key-to-path shape, and it is why this round does not move REMAINING and says so.

THE ROUND OPENED BY WITHDRAWING A CLAIM. R2576's report ended with "MILESTONE REACHED", and it was wrong: this run's milestone is to build ONE atom PARTIAL -> COMPLETE with `audit-catalog-status.sh`'s REMAINING as the oracle, and that number was 47 before R2576 and 47 after. Recorded here rather than only in a reply, because the same substitution is available to every later round: the milestone file says the round's prose does not decide this, the number does.
WHAT THE BASE TURNED OUT TO BE, and it is not upstream. `session-matching` carries three surviving witness gaps, and the first of them is not a witness gap at all: "a bare `get_matching_status()` poll with no listener declared registers no interest, so behind a router the REMOTE half of the poll still sees an empty set". Measured rather than quoted: `crates/wz-runtime-tokio/src/session/publisher.rs` @ `pub fn declare_matching_listener(` emits an Interest, while @ `pub fn get_matching_status(` emits no wire frame at all -- so the poll was reading a registry that nothing had asked the neighbour to fill. Both upstreams ask at PUBLISHER-DECLARE instead, and wz could not: `crates/wz-runtime-tokio/src/session/mod.rs` @ `pub fn declare_publisher(` returns an infallible by-value handle with no id and no undeclare, and that handle is `Clone` with NO `Drop`. The blocker was a TYPE SHAPE in this repository, so the milestone's "base is upstream -> register and stop" clause does not apply and the honest move was to build it.
THE REPAIR IS UPSTREAM'S OWN, AND THE `Clone` IS WHY. The obvious fix -- retract on drop -- is wrong here: a clone falling out of scope would cut a live publisher's interest. zenoh has exactly this problem and solves it by asking whether any other publisher still holds the resource before sending `InterestMode::Final` (`zenoh/src/api/session.rs` @ `pub(crate) fn undeclare_publisher_inner(`). So the COUNT moved to the session, keyed by `(plane, keyexpr)`: `Clone` takes a reference, `Drop` releases one, and only the last release retracts.
BOTH PLANES LANDED TOGETHER BECAUSE THEY ARE ONE SEAM. `Querier` has the identical shape and the identical defect on the QUERYABLES plane, and zenoh-pico makes both asks from the same helper (`vendor/zenoh-pico/src/api/api.c` @ `_z_write_filter_create(zs, &pub->_val._filter` and @ `_z_write_filter_create(zs, &querier->_val._filter`). Two tables would have been two things to keep in step; one table keyed by plane is the same mechanism twice, and the plane mix-up that design could introduce is pinned by a test rather than trusted.
A CONTROL CAME BACK GREEN AND THAT WAS THE ROUND'S SHARPEST MOMENT. Collapsing the plane key in the RELEASE path alone left the plane-separation test PASSING -- because for a publisher that collapse coincides with the correct key, so the probe never touched the claim. It had to damage BOTH sides before it redded. A control that comes back green is a finding about the control, and this one would have shipped a test believed to be load-bearing and was not.

Round 2578.decision_summary:
THE LEG THIS ROUND SET OUT TO BUILD IS TAGGED `wz-proves: none`, AND THAT IS THE ROUND'S RESULT RATHER THAN ITS FAILURE. §5.4 `session-matching` carries "a bare `get_matching_status()` poll with no listener declared registers no interest, so behind a router the REMOTE half of the poll still sees an empty set". R2577 had moved the ask to `Session::declare_publisher` under `cfg(all(session-matching, declare-interest))`, so a poll-only leg through a real zenohd should have been that clause's closer: remove the ask and the poll should never rise. MEASURED, with the demo rebuilt locally for every probe: removing the declare-time ask ENTIRELY leaves the leg green.
THE FIRST CONTROL WAS WORTHLESS AND THE DEMO'S OWN LOG SAID SO. `DECLARED MATCHING LISTENER` appeared in a run that never passed `--matching-log`, because the knob had been routed through `matching_publisher_keyexpr` -- a parameter meaning "declare a publisher AND its matching listener". So `--matching-poll` silently installed a listener whose own Interest answered the poll, and every damage to the publisher's ask was invisible. The wiring is now split: the keyexpr means "declare a publisher", which either knob wants, and a separate flag means "and watch it", which only one does. The contradiction was in plain text throughout and surfaced only when the leg was forced to dump its capture by awaiting a string that never appears.
WITH THAT FIXED THE RESULT HELD, AND THE NEGATIVE WAS CONFIRMED RATHER THAN ASSUMED: declare-time ask removed, `DECLARED MATCHING LISTENER` absent (grep count ZERO), and the bare poll still transitions `false` -> `true`. A stock zenohd tells an UNASKING CLIENT FACE about a remote subscriber. The residual's premise is therefore false for this topology at the pin.
SO THE LEG CANNOT CLAIM THE ATOM. A claim must bind to the atom's own gated code, and this verdict is identical with that code inert. Tagging it `session-matching` would have added a THIRD instance of exactly the defect R2577 found in two neighbouring legs of `wz_querier_all_complete_vs_pico_queryable.rs`, in the same round that named it. It is kept, tagged `none` with the measurement as its reason, because it still pins something real: a cold ask through a real router answers BY TRANSITION rather than by a latched initial value.
ONE ASYMMETRY IS UNEXPLAINED AND LEFT SO, DELIBERATELY. Under the same damage the sibling LISTENER leg still times out at 25s, so its documented control holds while the poll's does not -- two paths reading one registry disagree about whether the interest is load-bearing. The untested hypothesis is that emitting a WRONG-KIND interest is worse than emitting none, because it may consume the initial-interest slot. That is zenohd's forwarding policy, not wz's code: the base is UPSTREAM, so it was registered and a question asked rather than patched here. Inventing a dependency in wz to make the leg red would have been fabricating the very thing the measurement denies.
WHAT R2577's BUILD KEEPS. The declare-time ask is correct PARITY -- `zenoh/src/api/session.rs` @ `pub(crate) fn declare_publisher_inner(` and zenoh-pico's `z_declare_publisher` both ask there -- and it remains load-bearing for a face served by a peer or broker hat, where `.remote_interests` genuinely gates. Only the claim that it closes residual (1) is unsupported, and only for a wz client of a zenohd router.
A FIFTH COPY OF ONE WRONG SENTENCE. `hat/router/pubsub.rs:120-125` was cited as the mechanism by which a router withholds a declaration; at the pin that file carries no interest logic at all. This round repaired the copy in `run-ci.sh`'s own lane comment, after R2577 repaired four others. Every one was found because something else brought a reader to the file -- never by looking.

The sentence was repaired so the claim is now ADJUDICATED against `cargo metadata` rather than declared unresolvable -- the edge it states is real and direct.
THE FINDING IS THAT THE GATE BUILT TWO ROUNDS AGO TO PREVENT EXACTLY THIS WAS STANDING AND SAID NOTHING. `round_fed_gate_reach.py` exists to name every gate that a round's own changes feed and that the pre-push hook does not run. The rule had been written as A LIST OF THE TWO SUBJECTS ITS TWO INSTANCES HAPPENED TO SHARE rather than as the class, and a population defined by the examples in hand cannot report the example it does not have.
SO THE BASE IS THE DERIVATION, NOT THE SENTENCE. The class is one sentence -- a gate is round-fed when it ENUMERATES TRACKED FILES, because tracked files are what a round changes -- and it now has two spellings, both read from the AST: an invocation of `git ls-files`, which IS this repository's own enumerator of exactly that set, and a glob under a string constant whose first path segment is a tracked top-level directory. THE PLANE WAS MODELLED AS TWO AD-HOC MAPS AND THAT IS ONE DECISION WITH ELEVEN CONSEQUENCES. `FaceEntry` carries EIGHT declaration slots -- subs, qbls, tokens, live_subs, matches, adv_pubs, adv_subs, plus the session itself. The face-independent local plane carried TWO: `Inner.local_subs` and `Inner.local_qbls`. The six slots it did not have are exactly the eleven call sites that walked `faces.values_mut()` and skipped it. That is not eleven oversights to fix one at a time; a declaration site had to REMEMBER the plane, and most did not, because there was nowhere to put the handle if it had.
SO THE PLANE IS NOW A `FaceEntry` AND THERE IS ONE WALK. `Inner::declaration_targets()` names every session a declaration reaches -- the faces, and the plane -- and all eleven sites use it. Being correct now costs a site nothing and being wrong is no longer expressible. `declaration_targets_ref` is its shared-reference twin for the advanced publisher's put and delete, which reach handles they do not mutate; two methods because `&` and `&mut` cannot be one in Rust, never because they may name different sets.
THE PLANE IS DELIBERATELY NOT A MEMBER OF `faces`, AND THAT IS THE OTHER HALF. Five readers walk that map for a WIRE question -- `face_snapshots` and `peer_identities` answer about transports, and the three `batch_*` fans drive a window that exists per link -- and all five are correct as they stand. Keeping the plane out means they need no exclusion clause: the narrow meaning stays the default exactly where it is the right one, instead of becoming a list that rots.
ONE FIELD HAD TO SOFTEN AND IT WAS ARGUED ON ITS OWN TERMS. `FaceEntry::runtime` became `Option<Handle>`, because the plane is built in `SharedSession::new`, which runs on the C APPLICATION thread where `Handle::current()` PANICS. `None` means "this face captured no runtime", not "the runtime is gone", and the two `enter()` sites simply do not enter. That is sound on the field's own documented terms: its contract is "any declaration that spawns", and R2366 already moved the one measured spawner -- the advanced publisher's beacon -- onto the process partition, so it no longer asks the caller's thread for one. A real face still captures `Some` at `face_up`.

HOSTED LAYER C0 HAD BEEN DYING FOR FIVE PUSHES ON A DEFECT R2577 WROTE, AND NO LOCAL GATE COULD SEE IT. FINDING IT TOOK READING THE SEQUENCE, NOT THE WORD. The failing job's log is saturated with selftest fixture arms that print FAIL by design -- armed-skip, lane-reach, bump-sweep, doc-revision-consumer-pin, oracle-pin-gate -- and even the workflow's `##[error]` annotation was one, followed by `rc=1 want=fail ok`. What worked was reading which gate ran LAST before `ERROR Layer C0 FAIL`, because a fail-fast layer stops at the first genuine `return 1`; the line that named the real defect said `SELFTEST FAIL` about a real file and read like a fixture arm. Reproduced locally: `--selftest` rc=1.
THE INSTANCE IS REPAIRED BY DOING WHAT THE COMMENT ALREADY SAID: describing the two hat files instead of quoting their paths. `--selftest` rc=0 and `--check` still exactly on every budget, so the two rooted citations removed from a gate's own comment move no counted form.
THE BASE IS THAT A GATE'S SELFTEST RAN ONLY WHERE NOBODY WROTE THE GATE. A selftest validates the gate's own logic, and that logic only changes when the gate's source changes -- so the right population is exactly the gate modules a push edits. Running every selftest on every push would pay for 80-odd suites to grade untouched files; running none locally is what let this survive five rounds. New pre-push gate 5b runs `--selftest` for each edited `scripts/lib` module that carries the arm, placed before gate 3 for gate 5's reason: gate 3 exits early on a push touching no crate, and a push editing only gate sources is exactly that push.
THE MEMBERSHIP RULE THAT LOOKED STRICTER WAS THE WRONG ONE, MEASURED. Over all 136 modules, 81 carry `--selftest` as a code constant and none carry it only in text. A tighter rule -- "accepts it via an argparse `add_argument` or a direct compare" -- matched 77, and the four it dropped were then RUN with `--selftest`: all four accepted it and passed. So the stricter rule would have silently skipped real selftests, encoding the dispatch shapes its author thought of. The looser rule's only possible error is a module naming the constant without accepting it, which fails LOUDLY as an unknown argument -- the safe direction for a gate to err in.

The IPv6 multicast gap was generated by a TYPE, not by a missing call. `UdpDriver::bind_multicast_v4` and `UdpDriver::bind_multicast_tx_v4` took `group: Ipv4Addr`, so no caller could express a v6 group, and the demo's `--multicast-locator` refusal of IPv6 existed only because of that signature. Round 2587.decision_summary:
Milestone: build one atom PARTIAL -> COMPLETE. `transport-link-udp` (REMAINING WORK 46). The `ttl` foreign witness was the residual this atom's record said could not be built without an owner decision on a multicast-routing daemon. That premise was re-measured before anything else was touched, and it did not hold.

A routed hop is what witnessing a datagram's REACH needs, because reach is the kernel forwarding. The `ttl` key controls something narrower and implementation-owned: the value written into the IP header by `IP_MULTICAST_TTL` on the sending socket. Across one veth link that field arrives undecremented. Measured with zenohd and a raw `IP_RECVTTL` reader in a namespace, it read 5 with `ttl=5` and 1 without. So the question put to the owner rested on conflating two observables, and the right witness is a differential on the header field with zenohd as the adjudicator, not a new system dependency. Reach is explicitly not claimed.

The reader has to be independent of both implementations and run inside the namespace. It is plain libc in the shared test module, executed by re-running the test binary itself with `--exact` (the harness shape `layer3_keyexpr_canon.rs` established), since a second binary target would be one more artifact to build and locate. `sudo` resets the environment, so the request travels as an `env` argument. Without the request, the entry calibrates the reader against two TTLs it sets itself, so a reader stuck on one number cannot pass.

The wz side uses the demo's `--multicast-locator` run-mode flag, not the library, so the same leg is the key's first process-level witness. The first run read nothing from wz and the demo's own log said why: Layer M's router build lacked `locator-iface`, so `#iface=` only warned. The build was fixed rather than the test.

A correction is recorded rather than carried. R2584 and R2586 said the demo's scouting address silently falls back for an IPv6 value. It is refused at both boundaries, so the divergence is real but belongs to `scouting-active`.

Round 2592.decision_summary:
Build the per-link-kind socket configuration layer that upstream merges under every endpoint, which wz lacked entirely, before mapping any config-file key onto it.
- The base was structural. Upstream's transport manager keeps one parameter string per link kind, rendered from the zenoh config by each link's `ConfigurationInspector`, and layers every endpoint's own parameters over it on every dial and listen. wz had nowhere to hold a value for a whole link kind, so honouring `transport/link/tcp/so_*` from a file had no destination.
- `LinkDefaults` carries one `LinkSocketOptions` per kind and rides `DialConfig` and `AcceptConfig`. `LinkSocket::resolve` takes it as a second input and merges key by key before any reader decision, so refusals judge the merged set as upstream's do.
- The layer refuses keys upstream's inspectors never put there (for example `bind`). Accepting them would make it a wz-only capability rather than upstream's layer.
- In the demo the layer lives in `TransportTuning`, the bundle made to keep `transport/link` knobs off the run-mode signatures. It stops being `Copy`, and `demo_session_init_params` now borrows it. Every dial and accept config is built by the two builders, which now take the defaults; the reconnecting client and the storage host, which used bare defaults, now go through them too.
- The config-file mapping is left for the next round: it is a separate seam (`ZenohNodeConfig`, the honoured-key lists, the expansion) with its own gates.

THE FIVE `*_raw` FORMS ARE ONE SEAM, AND THE BASE IS THAT WZ HAS NO MATERIAL LAYER AT ALL -- measured, and the measurement REFUTED THIS ROUND'S FIRST READING, which is recorded rather than dropped. The first reading was that upstream resolves material per endpoint and that a per-key merge "would be the wrong mirror for wz". The second half is false. Upstream's precedence is TWO stages, not one: the config file's TLS section becomes a parameter string, then the endpoint's OWN parameters overwrite it KEY BY KEY -- upstream says so in its own comment, on both the listen and the dial path (`io/zenoh-transport/src/unicast/manager.rs` @ `// Overwrite config with current endpoint parameters`) -- and only then does one reader resolve raw over base64 over file (`io/zenoh-link-commons/src/quic/utils.rs` @ `async fn load_tls_certificate(`). So upstream merges at the level of MATERIAL and builds the rustls config last.

WHERE WZ DIVERGES, AND WHY THAT IS THE STRUCTURE TO ADD. wz has no material level: the caller hands in an already-built rustls config (`crates/wz-runtime-tokio/src/session_open.rs` @ `pub struct QuicDialConfig {`), and a built config cannot be merged key by key with anything. That is why the repair is not "let the locator override the config" but "give wz the layer upstream has" -- resolve MATERIAL (root CA, the listen pair, the connect pair) from locator-raw, then locator-base64/file, then the caller's configured source, and build the rustls config at the END from whatever that resolution produced. Bolting the five keys onto the existing built-config arms would reproduce the defect one level down: a locator naming only `root_ca_certificate_raw` would have to either discard the caller's listen material or ignore its own, and upstream does neither.

THE NEXT ROUND'S POPULATION IS TWELVE ARMS AND IT IS DERIVED, NOT LISTED: every site that consumes pre-built material spells `match &cfg.tls` or `match &cfg.quic`, and there are twelve of them -- three schemes (tls, quic, quic-datagram) times two sides (`crates/wz-runtime-tokio/src/session_open.rs` @ `pub async fn dial_locator(locator: AnyLocator, cfg: &DialConfig) -> io::Result<DialedLink> {` and `crates/wz-runtime-tokio/src/session_open.rs` @ `pub async fn bind_locator(locator: AnyLocator, cfg: &AcceptConfig) -> io::Result<BoundListener> {`) times two locator forms, the numeric `Ip` arm and the `Named` one. Twelve arms is why the repair must be ONE resolver the arms go through, the way `LinkSocket::resolve` is for the socket keys: a per-arm read is twelve chances to forget one, and the `Named` half is where a scheme has been forgotten before. It also changes what the `None` arm MEANS -- a locator carrying its own full material needs no caller config, so the typed `Unsupported` those arms return today is no longer the only answer when `cfg` is absent.

THE LOCATOR GRAMMAR ALREADY CARRIES A PEM, measured rather than assumed, so the next round has no grammar work to do: the config span splits on `;` and then on the FIRST `=` (`crates/wz-session-core/src/locator.rs` @ `fn lookup_param_all<'a>(params: &'a str, key: &'a str) -> impl Iterator<Item = &'a str> {`), so base64 padding and PEM newlines both survive inside a value, and an unknown key is IGNORED rather than refused -- which is exactly what `#root_ca_certificate_raw=` does today, parsed and dropped. The material must be BOXED when it lands: `AnyLocator` is pinned under 128 bytes (`crates/wz-session-core/src/locator.rs` @ `fn a_locator_stays_small_enough_to_hand_back_by_value() {`) because `mesh_dial_plan` hands one back inside a `Result` and clippy refuses a large `Err`.

WHAT `close_link_on_expiration` IS, measured against the pin rather than inferred from its name. After the handshake upstream takes the MINIMUM `not_after` over the peer chain (`io/zenoh-link-commons/src/quic/utils.rs` @ `pub fn get_cert_chain_expiration(conn: &quinn::Connection) -> ZResult<Option<OffsetDateTime>> {`) and, only when the key is true, spawns a task that closes the link at that instant (`io/zenoh-link-commons/src/tls.rs` @ `pub struct LinkCertExpirationManager {`). Its sleep is chunked at 600s against long-duration `tokio::time::sleep` unsoundness, and the close is guarded by a `set_closing` swap so the expiry task and a transport-initiated close cannot both run it. That is a link LIFETIME rather than a config source, so it is its own round and not a rider on the material one.

Do NOT file this as a wz gap -- the value reaches quinn by the only route there is, and that line's control is that deleting it fails to compile its caller.

`crates/wz-runtime-tokio/src/stream_link.rs` gains `ExpirySignal` and the race in `poll_event`. The signal carries BOTH a fired flag and a `Notify`, and needs both: a signal that fires while the driver is between polls has no waiter to notify, and a bool alone cannot wake a parked read. The round did NOT copy the quic implementation, because R2607 established by reading the code that it cannot be copied: quic arms by cloning a `quinn::Connection` and closing it, and its own comment says wz "already carries the signal" -- true of quic and ONLY of quic. `wire_tls_stream` takes the stream by value and `tokio::io::split` leaves no cloneable handle behind, which is exactly why upstream carries a cancellation-token module for tls and not for quic. Repair a HOSTED-ONLY defect R2624 introduced, at the level that stops it
recurring, and record a vacuity R2625 found by accident.

THE PER-PROJECT FIX WAS REFUSED. Adding `oracles/future-stamp -> target` to the
cache list works and needs a new line for every oracle ever added, which is a
rule with nothing holding it. `oracles/` is now a cargo WORKSPACE: one shared

editing, and a second oracle linking the same pinned zenoh REUSES those compiled
artifacts instead of paying its own cold build. The two workspaces stay separate
-- `crates/` is wz's, `oracles/` is the upstream-linked one -- which is what
keeps zenoh out of wz's dependency graph.

against the previous round's `--features router-hat-router` build (no `time-hlc`)
and the ABSORB leg PASSED. The reason is structural: with the clock compiled out
`treat_timestamp` does nothing, so the sample is relayed unchanged -- which is
exactly what a working ABSORB produces. Equality cannot separate "absorbed
correctly" from "no clock at all".

That is not a flaw to fix in the leg; it is a fact about what equality can
witness, and it is now written where a reader meets it. The leg's discriminating
partner is the REPLACE leg, which reds both ways, and the `time-hlc` build axis
is witnessed by the negative twin. The point generalises: every leg needs its own
twin, and this one's is a sibling leg rather than a build variant. An accident
produced the measurement; discarding it would have left a leg that reads stronger
than it is.

trio and AutoConnect, config-sourced link weights and their hot-reload, and the
links_info weight map. At the pin the router hat still reads
`routing.router.linkstate.transport_weights` at init and again on a config

THE BASE WAS A MISSING STRUCTURE, not a missing call site. The reason names
"zero call sites", which reads like a wiring gap, but there was nothing to
wire: `LinkstateNetwork::add_link` hardcoded the unset weight and the graph had
no place a configured weight could live, so a config parser landing first would
have had no receiver. This round builds the receiver, at the graph, shared by
both forwarders, and exposes it only where upstream does: the routers network.
The peers tier takes no weight whatever the map names.

`update_link_weights` is upstream's, clause for clause: a link moves only when
its entry in the OLD map differs from the NEW one; the map is stored whether or
not anything moved, so a later neighbour reads it; a graph in neither linkstate

Round 2639.decision_summary:
The queue had become a hiding place, and pre-push gate 2c was passing every push while three finished runs stood red.

MEASURED 2026-09-15. Hosted verdicts were arriving about eight hours after the push that created them, with eleven runs queued at once. Gate 2c grades the hosted run of the commit being replaced; at that depth EVERY push found its predecessor pending, and the PENDING arm passes by design -- correctly, because the standing rule is push-and-continue and the next push grades it. What it also did was report nothing else, so "the gate found no red" and "the gate measured nothing" printed the same. Meanwhile the three most recent runs that had actually finished were all red, two of them on one defect that went eleven rounds unrecorded, and the only reason anyone looked was that this session read `gh run list --status completed` by hand.

THE FIX KEEPS THE RULE AND REMOVES THE HIDING PLACE. When the immediate predecessor has not finished, the gate now grades the NEWEST RUN ON THIS HISTORY THAT HAS. It still never waits and never blames a run that is still going; it looks further back for something that actually graded. A red found that way refuses the push through the existing path -- same message, same failing-job listing, same per-run `WZ_ACK_RED` acknowledgement -- so the escape that keeps the fix pushable is unchanged.

WHY THE ANCESTOR SET IS PART OF THE PREDICATE. A run's head commit may belong to another branch, and grading such a run would blame this push for someone else's red. Only runs whose head commit is an ancestor of the commit under grade are considered, and an empty candidate set yields NONE rather than a pass: a population of zero is not a green, which is the shape this gate exists to refuse.

This round pays open-debt 734's shape (gate 2c reads `queued` as a pass) for the red half. It does NOT make the gate wait, and it does not fix the queue depth itself, which is unmeasured and account-level.

Round 2643.decision_summary:
The second round on `config-mutate-runtime`, and it builds the thing whose ABSENCE generates all three of that atom's residuals. REMAINING does not move: 35 before, 35 after, and this entry says so rather than letting a working seam read as a closed residual.

WHAT WAS MISSING, and it is one step deeper than "no write engine". wz had two representations of its configuration and nothing joining them. On one side a DOCUMENT type that parses a stock zenoh config, refuses unknown keys by name, records which keys the document actually stated, and emits itself back — with a test already witnessing that the emit and the ingest are inverses over the honoured keys. On the other side the LIVE config, a struct of typed fields carrying the runtime state. Between them: nothing. The document was parsed at startup, its values were poured into builder calls BY HAND at each host — the demo runner spells `.with_interceptors(..)` and `.with_admin_permissions(..)` one key at a time — and then the document was discarded.

WHY THAT IS THE GENERATOR RATHER THAN AN INSTANCE. Upstream's `Config` IS the document, with typed accessors over it, which is exactly what lets `insert_json5(key, value)` reach any path, what lets a key be deleted, and what gives the notifier something to announce. wz cannot splice a key into a document it no longer holds, so every runtime-mutable key has had to be paid for individually with a bespoke setter plus a host edit. That is why the measured surface is 3 runtime-mutable keys against 52 honoured ones — not a design preference for typed fields, but the absence of a document to write into.

WHAT THIS ROUND BUILT. `WzConfig::apply_zenoh_config` is the first declared mapping from a parsed document to the live config: one place that says which document key lands in which live slice, driven by the registry the previous round derived rather than by a second hand-written list. It is also the piece the full design needs regardless of how the write is spelled, because after splicing a key and re-ingesting, SOMETHING has to re-derive the live config, and that something is this function.

TWO RULES, BOTH FORCED BY MEASUREMENT RATHER THAN CHOSEN. It reads the document's STATED key set rather than the merged values, because the merged value of a key nobody wrote is a default, and the ingest type's own doc says a caller acting on it "would carry a decision the operator never made". And it applies PER KEY rather than per slice, because two keys share the adminspace-permissions slice and the parser fills the unstated one with a default — so a per-slice apply driven by a document naming only `read` would silently reset `write`. The second rule is not an argument; it is a test, and reverting to the per-slice shape reddens exactly that test by name.

WHAT IT DELIBERATELY DOES NOT DO. It stores; it does not push. For a push-discipline slice the consumer holds compiled state and reaching it is `reconfigure_*`'s job through a sink, so this is the STARTUP half of the join, before any sink exists. Calling it on a running node would store a value no consumer has seen, and the doc says so at the function rather than here.

The third round on `config-mutate-runtime`, and the one that makes a runtime config write REACHABLE rather than merely possible. REMAINING does not move: 35 before, 35 after. What exists now is the shape upstream's admin PUT has and wz did not.

UPSTREAM HAS ONE SHAPE AND WZ HAD N. An upstream admin PUT carries the config key as the path suffix and the value as the payload, and refuses an unknown path at insert. wz grew a bespoke sub-key per capability instead — `acl-deny`, `storage-add`, `storage-del`, `connect-add`, `admin-read` — each costing a decoder arm, an intent variant and a host arm. That per-key cost is the same one the registry was built to end, and this round found its sharpest instance: `admin-read` is a hand-rolled intent for `adminspace/permissions/read`, which is one of the three keys the registry already declares. Its own comment says so — "the one sub-key here that names a key UPSTREAM's config document also carries". It stays, because a foreign client speaks it and a lane witnesses it, but it is marked in the enum as the legacy spelling rather than the shape to copy.

WHAT LANDED. `WzConfig::set_by_key(key, value)` builds a NESTED one-key document from the key path, hands it to the ordinary reader — so the acceptance boundary, the type check and the unknown-key refusal are the reader's rather than a second implementation of them — and then to the document-to-live mapping the previous round built, where exactly one key is stated and so exactly one key is applied. `AdminConfigWrite::SetKey` carries the two halves from the wire, and the storage host's subscriber applies it against the live config it already locks for `admin-read`.

THE LAYERING IS FORCED, NOT CHOSEN, and it is written at both ends. The registry lives in the crate that DEPENDS on the one holding the decoder, so the decoder structurally cannot validate a key. It therefore passes both halves through as data and the runtime refuses by name when it applies — the same shape-here/apply-there split every other arm in that decoder already uses.

THREE REFUSALS, KEPT DISTINCT, and the first draft collapsed two of them until a test said so. A key wz has never heard of, a key it knows and deliberately does not honour, and a key it reads at startup but cannot change while running are three different answers to an operator. The middle one exists because the reader ACCEPTS an unhonoured key — a stock zenoh document carries many, and refusing the whole document over one would be wrong — and reports it as ignored instead. Answering that with "not runtime-mutable" would have told someone writing `downsampling` that wz reads the key, which it does not.

BOTH WIRE-FACING HALVES ARE INJECTION-GUARDED, because both arrive from the wire and both are spliced into a document this code assembles. Key segments must be `[A-Za-z0-9_]+`, so a segment cannot carry a quote and close the object early. The value is parsed as a standalone JSON5 value before it is embedded, so a payload carrying a trailing member cannot smuggle a second key in beside the one the caller named.

THE BOUND THIS DRAWS IS STATED RATHER THAN HIDDEN. The decoder routes on the presence of `/`, so a single-segment config key still reaches the unknown-sub-key answer. Measured: the only single-segment keys in the registry today are ones wz does not honour, so both routes end in a refusal that names the key and the bound is currently inert. It stops being inert the day a single-segment key becomes honoured AND runtime-mutable, and the fix then is a distinct wire prefix rather than a guess in a decoder that cannot see the registry.

Round 2645.decision_summary:
A host stopped re-implementing the admin answerer. REMAINING does not move — 35 before, 35 after — and the residual this round set out to close SURVIVES, measured rather than assumed. Both halves of that sentence are the entry's point.

WHAT WAS STRUCTURALLY WRONG. The library's adminspace declare took exactly ONE live input — a permissions source — and froze everything else at declare time: the config rendering, the plugin registry, the stats report. That is correct for a pure-Session host, whose handshake params are fixed for the session's life. It is wrong for a node that HOSTS an adminspace: its config can be rewritten over the wire, its dynamic registry reports whether a subsystem is actually live, and a mesh host deliberately serves NO stats because wz's counters are per-session and it holds N faces. Because the seam admitted one live input, the demo's storage host could not use it, so it built its own queryable and called the answerer itself. A re-implementation is exactly what the library's own per-GET witness cannot cover, which is how `adminspace-read` came to carry a residual saying the per-GET resolve had no witness THERE.

THE FIX IS THE SEAM, NOT THE CALLER. `AdminLiveInputs` names the whole set a hosting node re-reads, and `declare_adminspace_with_live_inputs` takes a source for it. The permissions-only method becomes a thin wrapper that computes its two frozen values exactly where it computed them before, so every existing caller sees what it saw. ONE call to the source per GET, never three closures: a reply must not pair a permit read at one instant with a config rendered at another, which is a property the storage host's own inline handler already protected and which three closures would have quietly lost.

STATS HAD TO JOIN THE LIVE SET, and that was a decision rather than a convenience. The demo's `None` is policy with a reason recorded at its own site: a mesh host has no counterpart to upstream's transport-manager aggregate, so serving one face's numbers as the node's would be a lie. A seam that resolved stats for the caller would force every such host to re-implement the answerer to say so — the very duplication this round removes, one field over.

THE COMPILER CONFIRMED THE DUPLICATION WAS REAL. Routing the host left `answer_admin_query`, `AdminAnswerCtx`, `QueryView`, `ReplyOut`, `queryable_key` and `get_zid` all unused. Six symbols existed only to serve a hand-rolled copy of a library path. The queryable key in particular was being derived twice from the same SSOT function; it is now derived once.

The faithful control — capture the same permit once at declare time, removing the liveness without changing the value — leaves all three E6i lanes GREEN, reproducing exactly what R2374 measured before this round existed. Routing moved that read into the library; it did not make anything observe it. `adminspace-read` therefore stays PARTIAL and is NOT re-graded here.

Round 2646.decision_summary:
Close `adminspace-write`'s DELETE residual at its base, refute its VALIDATOR residual against the pin, and name the residual that actually keeps the atom PARTIAL.

The delete half was not missing at the decoder the residual named. It was missing one level BELOW: both forwarder planes matched only a Put body in `dispatch_local_subscribers` and hardcoded `kind: SampleKind::Put`, so no forwarder-hosted local subscriber in this tree could observe a delete for ANY keyexpr. The forwarder still forwarded the Del onward, so a delete crossed the node correctly and vanished on the way to the node's own host -- invisible from the wire, which is why it survived. Fixing the decoder alone would have added an arm no message could reach.

The write gate then takes a BODY TYPE instead of a payload, so a delete cannot carry one and `(payload, is_delete)` is not representable; the key is matched first and the body second, which is upstream's order. The runtime applies a delete as a restore to the schema default through the SAME per-key table the set half uses, so a future registry key gets both halves from one edit rather than from two tables that must agree.

The validator residual is refuted rather than built. Measured at the pin, upstream's `ConfigValidator` seam is reachable only through the plugins field -- both call sites sit inside `impl PluginsConfig`, keyed by plugin name -- so an upstream write to `adminspace/permissions/read` passes no validator either. Building a hook for it would have been a mechanism with no reachable caller. The refutation is pinned as a control instead of written down, so it reds the day `plugins` becomes honoured.

What actually remains was measured while closing those two: the admin write surface is TWO BOOLEANS WIDE. Every other runtime-mutable key is push-discipline and refused by name, and upstream additionally accepts an array-member key form wz has no route for. That is one residual -- the surface is narrower than upstream's -- and it is why this atom stays PARTIAL rather than going COMPLETE.

Round 2647.decision_summary:
Repair the standing Layer Z red at its base — a RESTORED cache artifact is trusted without being read — and correct two atom reasons that had gone false about this tree's own code.

The red had a recorded diagnosis and it was wrong. The note said `build-zenohd.sh` prefers a cargo-git checkout over the pinned-tag clone, so the variants build off-pin. Re-measured, that cannot produce the symptom: the script asserts the SELECTED source's version against the pin and exits 1 on a mismatch, so an off-pin source fails the build loudly rather than shipping a divergent oracle.

The actual base is a missing structure rather than a wrong one. `ci.yml` restores each oracle from cache, builds it ONLY on a cache miss, and then checks it with `test -x` — presence. Nothing asks what the binary IS. The key merely NAMES 1.10.1: a promise made before the build, not a reading of what it produced. So a poisoned entry is restored for ever and `build-zenohd.sh`'s own version assert can never fire, because it lives inside the build that no longer runs. One such entry per variant has been hiding 77 of Layer Z's 78 legs.

The repair reads the binary and rebuilds when the answer is not the pin, and it DERIVES FROM THE GRADER rather than beside it: population, pin and classification are `oracle_pin_gate`'s own functions, and the two sets are asserted equal so repairer and grader cannot drift. The cache keys are bound to the repair script as well, which abandons the entries measured poisoned once and thereafter keeps the key moving with the logic that decides whether a restore is acceptable.
verification_bullets: THE REPAIR'S SELFTEST BITES IN BOTH DIRECTIONS, driven before the file was installed and re-run after: inverting `decide` reds on `decide(ABSENT)`, and disabling the guard match reds by NAMING the wrong pairing — the important one, because silently pairing every variant to `None` would rebuild the default oracle three times and leave every variant stale, which is a correct value on a wrong route. Six derivations drive: the decision table over all four verdicts, the pairing, a FIFTH variant covered with no edit here, the build command's variant and clone-opt-in, an empty population as a hard fail, and the pairing/gate disagreement.
THE INSTALLED COPY IS BYTE-IDENTICAL to the verified draft (`diff -q` reports no difference), so the verification above is about the file this commit carries and not about a text that resembles it.

MEASURED against the live tree: `--check` prints 4 oracles paired -- 1 default, 3 variant, pin 1.10.1, set agrees with `oracle_pin_gate`. `--plan` correctly marks all four local oracles for rebuild (they answer 1.10.0 against a 1.10.1 pin) with the right variant variable each.

Round 2650.decision_summary:
Closing this atom's residual means routing eight of the ten runtime-mutable
keys; R2649 routed the one whose slice is fed by it alone. The remaining seven

per-key write of any join input needs inputs the live slice does not retain.

So the two independent keys go first, and `low_pass_filter` first of those
because it is the flattest. That is a seam, not a size: it grades the reader

next round narrows to the structure rather than to the reader.

interceptor's rule type. The ingest struct is deliberately feature-independent
-- every build must read the same document to the same values -- and the rule
types are gated twice over. The trick that lets the weights field name a foreign
type does not reach here: a feature pulling a separate CRATE is available to any
build that turns it on, while these types sit behind a feature of this same

larger claim than reading a key.

Round 2651.decision_summary:
`downsampling` is the second and last interceptor key whose live slice is fed by
it ALONE, so it completes the half of this residual that needs no new structure.
The five `access_control/*` keys that remain collapse into a single field through
a join that cannot be inverted, and taking them next means building a retention
structure first -- which is why the two independent keys went first and together.

Its only new shape against its sibling is one level of nesting: upstream carries
a list of ITEMS, each holding the axes a group of rules share plus its own list
of rate rules, where the key expression is SINGULAR per rule. So one item expands
to one wz rule per rate rule, with the item's axes copied onto each. That is
upstream's own arrangement -- subject and kind selectors on the item, only the
rate varying -- so the reader re-spells it rather than reinterpreting it.

The frequency conversion was NOT written again. It already exists, public, with
both of its edges documented, and those edges are the reason a second copy would
have been a defect: a zero frequency is upstream's DROP-ALL rule rather than "no
throttle", and a negative or non-finite one saturates to no throttle at all. A
reader that restated either would have been a second opinion about upstream.
verification_bullets: RED-FIRST, on what is DISTINCTIVE rather than on what the previous key already
settled. Repeating the message-vocabulary damage would have proved nothing new,
so the probe truncated the NESTED rate rules to the first one. The test failed by
name on "both rate rules survive the parse" -- which is exactly the defect this
key's own drop-row reasoning warns about, a document's later rules vanishing with
nobody able to see that they did. Restored, the reader's module is 56 green and
the demo 60.
BOTH DIRECTIONS of the acceptance boundary are pinned by that one test, because a
reader can fail either way. Refusing a message kind from the access-control
vocabulary keeps wz from being LOOSER than upstream, in the direction the
stock-config lane structurally cannot see -- that lane only drives documents a
real zenohd already starts on. Accepting a zero rate keeps wz from being
STRICTER, and the assertion says why rather than leaving it to be rediscovered.
The four registry gates report green, and the honoured count moved 49 -> 50 with
the surface total unchanged, which is what a move between the halves of one
partition must look like. Both hosted-only obligations are paid from measurement
rather than inference: the drop-in fixture carries a shape a real zenohd was
observed to start on, and the defaults leg classes the key as comparable at the
empty list, which is what a silent zenohd renders.

Round 2657.decision_summary:
THE LAST CLAUSE IS BUILT AND IT WAS HIDING A SMALLER ONE. `adminspace-write`
stood on upstream's `<array>/<field>=<value>` member addressing; that form is
honoured now, both halves, for all six array-valued keys. It is a PREFIX STEP in
front of the write gate rather than a second gate, which is upstream's own
arrangement -- its admin handler tries the array route first and falls through
when the key carries no `=` -- so the acceptance boundary, the sink resolution,
the snapshot, the push and the rollback are the path a whole-array write already
takes.

THE SEMANTICS ARE UPSTREAM'S AND THE HALVES ARE NOT SYMMETRIC. An insert
replaces the FIRST match and appends when none matches; a remove drops EVERY
match. Nothing about the operation's name says which, and a round that
implemented one shape twice would have been wrong once. The comparison is
`serde_json`'s `as_str()`, so a NUMERIC field addresses nothing -- reproducing
that is what keeps the two acceptance boundaries the same, because a wz that
matched numerically would apply a write upstream refuses.

IT SPLICES THE RETAINED ARRAY, WHICH IS WHAT R2656 BUILT IT FOR. Upstream can
splice generically because its config IS a document; wz's is typed, so the
element goes through the slice's OWN parser as a one-element array and the
splice happens on the list the retention already holds.

⛔ AND READING THE DECODER TO WIRE IT UP FOUND THE CLAUSE THE CLAUSE WAS HIDING.
`parse_admin_config_write` routes a config path on `other.contains('/')`, so a
SINGLE-SEGMENT config key decodes `UnknownKey`. Its own comment declared that
bound inert "until a single-segment key becomes honoured AND runtime-mutable" --
R2651 honoured `downsampling` and `low_pass_filter`, R2654 made every
runtime-mutable key writable, and nobody came back. So a wire write to
`downsampling` is refused on a node that can apply it while `downsampling/id=x`
carries a slash and lands. The base is that wz overloaded ONE keyexpr space with
two vocabularies and used a slash as the discriminator; upstream has no action
names in that space at all.

R2658 -- the admin config-write decoder decides by VOCABULARY rather than by
the key's SHAPE, and the lane that grades that surface names the tests it runs.

THE BASE, first half. `parse_admin_config_write` classified a sub-key under
`@/<zid>/<whatami>/config/` by asking `subkey.contains('/')`: more than one
segment meant a config path, one segment meant an unknown key. The comment
above that arm admitted the bound and called it inert. It stopped being inert
two rounds ago -- R2651 honoured `downsampling` and `low_pass_filter`, R2654
made every runtime-mutable key writable through the sinks -- so a wire write to
`downsampling` answered `UnknownKey` on a node that could apply it, while its
MEMBER form `downsampling/id=x`, one `/` longer, decoded fine. A key whose
whole-value write is unreachable while one of its rows is reachable is not a
bound; it is a defect, and the shape heuristic generated it.

WHY THE HEURISTIC WAS THERE is the actual base: the decoder had no config-key
vocabulary. Its own comment says so -- the runtime-mutable registry lives in
`wz-runtime-tokio`, which depends on `wz-session-core` and not the reverse --
and a classifier with no vocabulary substitutes something that correlates with
one. So the vocabulary is now a PARAMETER (`is_config_key`), supplied by the
crate that owns the registry.

TWO GOALS HAD TO HOLD AT ONCE, and each of the two obvious repairs loses one.
(A) a single-segment upstream key must decode as a write; (B) R2644 pinned
`acl-denyy` -- a typo of `acl-deny` -- as `UnknownKey`, because a typo of a
bespoke sub-key that silently became a config write would be refused a whole
crate away under a different message. `contains('/')` buys (B) by losing (A);
a plain catch-all buys (A) by losing (B). A predicate buys both, because a typo
is in NEITHER vocabulary.

THE PREDICATE IS THE ACCEPTANCE BOUNDARY, NOT "does wz honour it". A key
upstream carries and wz deliberately ignores (`plugins`) must decode as a
config write so the runtime answers `NotHonoured` by name; a predicate narrowed
to "honoured" collapses R2644's three-way distinction (never-heard-of /
known-and-ignored / known-and-not-runtime-mutable) into two.

settled: `zenoh_config::wz_accepts` alone is NOT that boundary. It is a

decoder raw would have refused the very rows R2657 made writable -- a
regression of the previous round, introduced by the round that cites it.
`config::accepts_config_key` resolves the member form first, through the SAME
`classify_write_key` the write itself uses, so the two cannot answer
differently.

This round repairs open debt 758 at its base, and the base is not where the
item says it is. The item has now had THREE diagnoses and this is the first
one that survives measurement.

WHAT THE RED IS. Four consecutive hosted runs reduce to one failing step,
`Ensure the unixpipe zenohd ANSWERS at the pin`, with 20 of 21 jobs green.
The step is honest: the binary answers with a commit sha where the pin names a
version.

THE TWO EARLIER DIAGNOSES, and why each is wrong. (1) "the variants build
off-pin" -- refuted already, and correctly: the build asserts the SELECTED
source's version against the pin and exits on a mismatch, so an off-pin source
fails loudly instead of shipping a divergent oracle. (2) "a poisoned cache
entry is restored without being read" -- this is the item's current text, and
it is what `ensure_zenohd_at_pin.py` was built for. It is refuted by the run
itself: that reader RUNS, REBUILDS from the pinned source, and lands on the
IDENTICAL answer. A rebuild that reproduces the string is not a poisoned
restore, and no cache-key bump can reach it.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY TRUE, measured. `zenohd/src/main.rs` @ `const GIT_VERSION`
takes its string from the `git-version` crate's `git_version!` macro, which
shells out to `git describe` at BUILD time. A cargo git checkout is a detached
worktree cargo materialises by commit, and cargo does not fetch tags into it --
measured: `git tag` lists ZERO there while the same tree's `Cargo.toml` says
the pinned version. So that tree IS the pin and CANNOT SAY so. Since
`build-zenohd.sh` globs that checkout BEFORE its own tag clone, and
`oracles/future-stamp` declares zenoh as a cargo GIT dependency that
materialises it mid-job, the oracle's identity became a function of BUILD
ORDER: whichever oracle is built before that dependency resolves gets the tag
clone and answers the version, whichever is built after gets the checkout and
answers the sha. Run 35101414755 shows exactly that shape -- same job, same
pin, same `ZENOHD_ALLOW_CLONE=1`, and the default oracle MATCHes while the
variant is STALE.

THE REPAIR, placed where identity is decided rather than where it surfaced.
Immediately after `$ZH` is selected, the tree must be able to NAME the pin; if
it cannot and a clone is permitted, `$ZH` is cleared so the existing tag-clone
path runs. This keeps the developer affordance that clause was written for --
a plain clone handed over by `ZENOHD_SRC` still names its tag and is still
used -- and excludes exactly the tree that cannot answer.

derived `git describe --tags` in a previous round and recorded it as settled.
Measured here: `git-version` 0.3.9 documents its default as
`args = ["--always", "--dirty=-modified"]` -- with NO `--tags`, so only
ANNOTATED tags count. A check written with `--tags` would have ACCEPTED a tree
whose pin tag is lightweight, the build would still have fallen through to the
sha, and this same red would have returned having passed its own gate. The
predicate now runs the build's own invocation.

settled by a hosted run, not by this entry. What is proven is that the
selection can no longer hand the build a tree that cannot name the pin, and
that the discriminator refuses the real cargo checkout while accepting a
tagged tree.

attachment, both encodings, source_info and timestamp) and an UNBOUNDED channel,

answers are wrong: blocking stalls the drive loop that fires the deferred cell,
and dropping loses a reply a one-shot get can never be asked for again.

sweeps once -- upstream's per-query task in the shape wz's sweep already had.
It is a METHOD OF ITS OWN rather than a step inside the channel form, because
upstream reaps for both of its forms; the channel form calls it, and a
callback-form caller on an AP session calls it directly. The `Send + 'static`
bounds sit on these two methods, never on the impl block.

order `group.rs` takes for its watchdog. Checking after would leave a pending

Round 2678.decision_summary:
Build `session-close-ingress` by moving a REQUEST across the seam rather than
moving authority across it. The keyexpr matcher and the session FSM engine are
owned by different things and were never in scope together: the matcher runs
under the observer lock on the `Session` handle, whose `SessionInner` holds no
engine, and the engine is owned by `OpenedSession`, moved into the drive loop
and borrowed there for its whole life.

The obvious move was to widen the loop's `on_event` hook, which is called while
the loop holds the engine. It is refused, and not for its blast radius: that
hook is the application observer fan, and handing every app callback `&mut` on
the session's state machine grants authority the hook has no business granting.
So the request travels as data on the shared bundle and the raise stays where
the engine already is, beside `check_lease_deadline` — the only other production
site in this tree that raises a session FSM event.

The ingress carries no event-name literal. It asks the generated machine through
`StatePolicy::get_event_from_name`, because a name agreed by hand between two
places stays agreed only until one of them is edited — which is exactly the
defect open-debt item 777 was registered for one round earlier, in this same
tree, at a cost of one push.
