Round 2690.decision_summary:
Build the pure-Session admin host's per-entity introspection, the second
of the three residual families §5.23 names. The host passed
answer_admin_query a literal empty slice, so it reported "nothing is
declared" however much its face had declared to it.

The handler cannot read the tables it must report. It is stored INSIDE
the observer's queryable registry and dispatched with the observer
borrowed mutably, so it can neither borrow the registries back nor
re-lock the observer. The router host's answer -- a live view over its
tables -- does not transfer, because ITS tables are already shared cells
while the observer's are owned outright; giving them a shared cell would
put a synchronization primitive into no_std wz-session-core, which the
MCU profile has no answer for.

So the host reads a CACHE, and the cache is kept honest by construction
rather than by discipline: every write is a WHOLE-STATE rebuild from the
live tables, nothing patches it in place, and nothing reads its previous
value. What it holds is therefore always a state the tables actually
held. An incremental side-table fed by declaration sinks would be the
other thing -- a second source of truth that can miss a mutation and
then disagree indefinitely.

The refresh attaches to the two sites that MUTATE those tables, not to
one convenient site: the unicast dispatch SSOT, and the link-loss flush.
The second is the one a dispatch-only refresh could never cover -- on a
dead link there may be no further iteration event at all, and a local
admin GET would go on reporting a departed peer's subscriptions.

The declarations are resolved INSIDE the declare rather than added to
the AdminLiveInputs seam. The seam carries what a CALLER must choose; a
Session has exactly one face and every caller of that method is a
Session, so there is nothing to choose. On the seam it would be a field
each host must remember to fill, and the host that forgot would report
an empty table as confidently as the host with nothing to report.

Register the fifth per-entity leg, and close the structure that let it
stay unnamed.

THE LEG: upstream serves FIVE per-entity handlers through one helper --
subscriber, publisher, queryable, querier and token. This atom's reason
accounted for four and was silent about the token leg, which sits inside
its own declared upstream range. No other entry claims it either: a term
search over every inventory reason returns zero mentions of the handler.
So a round closing publisher/querier alone would not have moved the
grade, and the round before this one said it would.

WHY IT COULD HIDE, which is the part worth fixing rather than the
omission itself. The kind set lived in three places: the enum, the
surface manifest, and the fixture that feeds the manifest-versus-answerer
gate. That gate is strong -- it RUNS the answerer and compares both
directions -- but its population is the fixture, and its own comment says
why that matters. A kind in the enum and in neither list produces no
reply to compare and no leg to miss, so it is vacuous in both directions:
the gate stays green while the manifest under-reports, and the manifest
is the document a consumer reads to learn what a node answers.

So the manifest and the fixture now DERIVE from one kind set. Adding a
variant reaches both without anyone remembering to go there.

WHAT THIS DELIBERATELY DOES NOT CLAIM: the kind set is itself a
hand-written array and stable Rust cannot prove it names every variant. A
check that iterates it cannot catch an omission from it -- it never sees
the missing one. The exhaustive match beside it makes a new variant fail
to compile until it is given an arm, which puts the author in the block
where the array is; that is a prompt, not a proof, and it is recorded as
one.

Pay what R2691's own gates found, and correct what its entry claimed.

R2691 widened a public enum and its ledger entry said: "The workspace
type-checks whole. That is the check this change needed." That was

THE REPAIR WENT TO THE BASE AND THEN PAST IT, TWICE, WHICH IS THE PART
WORTH RECORDING. The stale `match` was an ordinal table -- a second copy
of the variant set, living one crate from the enum. First fix: derive
the ordinal from the kind set, so the copy stops existing. That removed
the duplicate and introduced a worse thing: an ordinal derived by
lookup needs an `expect`, and the invariant it guards is the one this
round had just documented as unprovable in stable Rust. A compile error
became a runtime panic.

Second fix, and the one that holds: derive `Ord` on the enum and key the
map by the kind itself. No ordinal, no reverse lookup, no panic, and
nothing left to keep in step. The earlier comment there had argued
against exactly this -- "making it `Ord` would widen a wz-session-core
public type for one consumer's map key" -- and that objection has now
been tested by events: avoiding the widening bought a stale copy, a
build break, and a panic. Deriving `Ord` on a fieldless enum is a trait
impl, not a representation change.

Round 2693.decision_summary:
The round set out to build the peer's TOKEN introspection leg, the second
of the three residual clauses on the adminspace-introspection-handlers
atom. It built that. Then the count guard refused the push, and what it
refused over turned out to be larger than the leg.

Decision 1 -- the token leg answers from the peer's own two tiers, and the
backer predicate is constantly false. The peer has no native token path at
all: its ingest advertises a CLIENT's token into the mesh under THIS node's
zid, so the mesh table holds a self row for a keyexpr this node does not
itself hold. That is the exact shape open-debt 779 was: a self row read as
a source. Passing `|_| false` is therefore not a stub, it is the true
predicate for this forwarder, and the control proves it carries weight --
inverting it to `|_| true` makes the node claim a token its client holds.

Decision 2 -- a test helper's `#[cfg]` is the CONSUMER's, spelled out, not
a wider gate that happens to contain it. This is the SECOND time in this
round that a helper gated more widely than its only caller broke a build
that turns the caller off; `-D dead-code` is what says so, and it says it
only in a configuration no lane this round had run. The narrow rule is
written at the helper now, so the next reader is told rather than left to
rediscover it.

Decision 3 -- the tests this atom rests on get a lane that RUNS them.
`adminspace-introspection-handlers` is not a default feature, so the
changed-crate hook gate never reached it, and in run-ci this layer named

WHY THE REPAIR IS A MERGE AND NOT A RE-KEY. Re-keying fixes both symptoms and leaves the generator: a second table beside the interest store is a second lifecycle maintained by hand, and two of its four operations were already wrong. Folding mesh faces into `FutureInterestStore` under a role tag makes replace, remove-one and remove-all the ones that type already implements — the `Interest(Final)` arm was already calling `remove_interest`, `deregister` already calling `purge_face`, the id key already last-wins. Only `insert` is new code.

THE RISK MOVES, AND IS PINNED WHERE IT MOVES TO. Three methods walk the store to push; a mesh face reaching one would declare onto a plane `flood_to_tree_children` already serves — a data-plane fault, worse than the reporting gap. So the filter is ONE private accessor the three share, with `by_face` private so they can be made to, rather than three conditionals anyone can forget.

Round 2696.decision_summary:
Build the volume half of the config-hotreload lifecycle, which this atom's
own reason names as the one residual a round may take -- and correct a false
clause R2693 left standing in a gate file.

WHY THIS RESIDUAL AND NOT ANOTHER. A survey derived from the oracle's own
REMAINING line (27 atoms, not a hand list) read each reason's tail. The
closest to COMPLETE is adminspace-config-hotreload, whose four residual
claims R2670 had already folded into ONE plus a scope question: three of them
(diff engine, validator seam, notification plane) sit behind upstream's
plugins feature and wait on open-debt item 773, which is registered as an
owner decision and says in its own body that a round must not settle it. The
fourth -- no volume lifecycle from the wire -- does not wait on it. It is
required under BOTH branches of that question: if wz accepts a declarative
document, AddVolume/DeleteVolume are what its diff would apply; if wz stays
intent-only, the intent path must carry volume lifecycle to be the superset
this reason calls it. That is why it could be taken without pre-empting the
owner.

THE BASE. Upstream's kill_volume stops every storage hosted on a volume
before stopping the volume, because a storage outliving its volume answers
out of a backend nothing can re-create. wz could not express the operation at
all: VolumeRegistry had insert, replace, lookup and enumerate and NO removal,
so a volume was a thing a node could only ever gain. The cascade cannot live
in the registry either -- it holds volumes and cannot see who resolved
through it -- so it belongs to RuntimeStorageManager, the one layer holding
both maps, with the hosted set DERIVED from each storage's own volume_id
rather than from a second volume-keyed index that would need keeping true.

WHAT WAS DELIBERATELY NOT BUILT. Upstream's VolumeConfig::paths names
libraries to dlopen. wz's dynamic-volume seam is a three-phase operator flow
whose refusals are operator errors reported before any volume is registered;
routing that through a per-client wire verb needs those decisions re-made for
a caller who cannot see the other clients' paths. Named in the intent's own
doc as a scope line rather than left as an omission.

verification_bullets: THREE FINDINGS, EACH WITH THE THING THAT PRODUCED IT.

refuted it in one line. "Enforcement needs a routing build" reads as a FEATURE
gap, and `pub mod interceptor` is indeed `#[cfg(feature = "routing-peer")]` --
which looked like the base until the feature table answered: `access-acl =
["routing-peer", ...]`. ACL cannot be enabled without routing-peer, so the
interceptor module is compiled in every build that can hold a policy at all.
The gap is an INSTANCE, not a feature. Upstream builds its enforcer per
TRANSPORT (`zenoh/src/net/routing/interceptor/access_control.rs` @
`fn new_transport_unicast(`) with no condition on the transport belonging to a
router; wz built it per forwarder.
(2) A CONTEXT WITHOUT ITS CONSUMER DOES NOT COMPILE, which is the compiler
stating the unit of work. The session-side `InterceptorContext` was written and
`-D dead-code` refused it: "struct `SessionContext` is never constructed". The
same class caught R2698's extractor. So the landable unit is context + chain +
the consult together, never the context alone.

`Interceptor` IS NOT `Send`. Putting the chain on the shared `SessionInner`
behind `R::Mutex` fails with "`(dyn Interceptor + 'static)` cannot be sent
between threads safely". The two forwarders get away with `RefCell` because a
forwarder is TASK-LOCAL; a `Session` handle is shared and its mutex demands
Send. So the chain is not session state at all -- it belongs with the drive
loop, or the session stores the Send `InterceptorConfig` and the loop owns the
chain built from it.

R2700 filed open-debt 782 after four placements for a client-mode ACL
chain were each refused by an existing boundary, and named the first
refusal without following it: the chain "cannot be sent between threads
safely". This round asked what that refusal is ABOUT rather than routing
around it, and the answer is upstream's own declaration. zenoh's
interceptor is `Box<dyn InterceptorTrait + Send + Sync>`; wz's trait
object carried no auto-trait bound at all. That is not a divergence
someone chose -- it is a bound nobody needed while the only holder of a
chain was task-local, and it silently decided who may ever hold one.

So the base is the SEAM, not the session. A `Cell` in the downsampling
rule timer -- picked because `intercept` takes `&self`, and defended in
its own doc by a correct argument about SHARING -- is what made the whole
trait unimplementable with `Sync`. The doc's argument was never wrong; it
was answering a different question than the one the field decides. A
field's interior-mutability choice is an assertion about who may hold the
TYPE, and upstream records the same conclusion by holding its per-rule
timestate behind a lock rather than a cell.

Fixing the seam is deliberately NOT fixing the atom. `access-acl` stays
PARTIAL: a chain that CAN be held by a session is not a session that
HOLDS one. What the round buys is that the next placement is no longer
refused before it is written.

The round also pays a stale clause found while re-reading the reason
rather than remembering it: R2698 built the cert-common-name subject axis
and never came back to the store, so the reason had asserted a missing
axis for three rounds while the code carried it.

Round 2702.decision_summary:
R2701 removed the type-level obstacle to holding an interceptor chain in
shared state. This round asked what the §5.16 seam's `routing-peer` gate
was actually FOR, and the answer was: one function. Nothing under
`interceptor/` names a routing type, but the enforcer's own governed
keyexpr resolver lived inside `linkstate_forward.rs`, so the seam could
not compile without a routing build. That is a gate whose cause is a file
placement, and `access-acl`'s residual has been quoting it for many
rounds as "wz gates the whole engine behind a routing build".

The move is the fix and the direction is the argument. A forwarder is a
CONSUMER of the seam -- it holds the chains, builds them, implements
`InterceptorSink` -- so a forwarder importing the seam's resolver adds no
edge, while the seam importing the forwarder's was an edge from a thing
into one of its own consumers. The two peer-identity readers moved for
the same reason and to a module named for what they are rather than for
either consumer: routing keys its graph on the zid, the enforcer reads
the same two values as subject axes, and neither owns them.

THE ROUND'S ORDER WAS DERIVED AND THEN REFUTED BY THE COMPILER, which is
worth recording because the refutation is the useful part. The plan was
to decompose the feature first and build the consultation second, so the
witness would run in the configuration the residual names. `-D dead-code`
refused that: an `access-acl` build with no consumer has a policy engine,
a resolver, and nothing that consults either. The seam and its
consultation are one landing unit, and the compiler said so more clearly
than the reasoning did.

So the session became the third `InterceptorContext` implementation and
the second `InterceptorSink`, and `access-acl` stopped naming
`routing-peer`. It names the codecs its enforcers actually read instead,
which is the difference between a dependency and a bundle.

INGRESS LANDED IN THE SAME ROUND, because it shares the seam and
splitting it would have bought two corrections to one reason. It needed a
seam of its own: the drive loop is the only place an inbound batch is
still OWNED -- `on_event` receives a BORROW, so by the time anything
downstream sees the batch the decision is already made -- and the loop
holds the link actions, not the session. So the loop gained an ingress
DECORATOR parameter and the session gained a decorator to hand it.

THE OBVIOUS CHEAPER PLACEMENT WAS TRIED AND REFUSED, which is why the
seam is the answer rather than a preference. Filtering at the session's
own inbound door (`dispatch_iteration_event_with`) would need no loop
change and would be symmetric with egress -- but it hands the whole batch
to `no_std` session-core in one call, UNDER the observer lock that the
verdict itself must take to resolve a keyexpr. Two walls, either of which
is fatal.

THEN THE ROUND ALMOST STOPPED ONE TEST SHORT, and the reason it did not
is the rule it would have broken. With both flows built, every part had a
witness and nothing had witnessed the JOIN: that the loop calls the
decorator at a point where the drop still matters. Both ends true and the
join unverified is a class this tree has paid for seven times, and a
call-count assertion would have been that mistake in miniature. So the
last piece is an end-to-end test that replays a REAL encoded frame --
captured by publishing the message and reading what this tree's own
encoder emitted -- through the production loop.

Round 2703.decision_summary:
Close rest-sse-subscribe's last residual at its base: give wz the
subscription-delivery abstraction it had none of, rather than making the
SSE bridge block where blocking is unsafe.

The reason set the order itself -- "adopting FIFO block-when-full is only
correct AFTER delivery leaves the drive loop" -- and that was a statement
about a missing structure, not a missing constant. A subscriber callback
runs INLINE on the one drive loop, so the bridge could not block where it
received; every consumer needing a queue therefore dropped on overflow,
which contradicted this tree's own TX-side ruling that the peer's
backpressure IS the flow control and cutting a write short is the same
data loss in a different place.

So delivery gets a two-stage seam: a callback that stages without waiting,
and a drain the LOOP awaits. The wait then sits at a suspension point of
the loop instead of inside a callback the loop calls inline.

The second decision is the one that makes the first honest. Keepalive TX
is emitted BY that same loop and there is no timer task to fall back on,
so a bare await would have silenced keepalive for as long as a consumer
lagged and let the peer expire a healthy session -- a lost sample traded
for a lost session, which is a worse divergence wearing parity's name.
The wait therefore happens inside a park that races the drain against the
same lease and keepalive wake the loop head arms. Upstream gets this for
free because its blocking handler parks one link's rx task while keepalive
runs on another; wz has one loop, so it keeps the duty running by hand.

2. Liveness. A consumer that NEVER reads: the witness requires the parked
loop to keep emitting keepalive. Control (park takes the plain-await
path) FAILED with "got 0"; witness ok. Under that same control the
backpressure witness stayed green, so the two witnesses are independent
and each control moves exactly one of them.

round's most useful finding. The loop drains after EVERY frame, so the

Round 2705.decision_summary:
A hosted red paid at its base, and the base is one line of default behaviour.

Layer Z's `wz_rest_sse_renders_the_same_sample_as_the_zenohd_rest_plugin` failed on TWO consecutive runs, and the second ran on a tree that already carried R2703's fix -- so the earlier reading, that the red predated the repair, was wrong. Ordering was re-measured: the failing run's head commit is a DESCENDANT of the round that graded `rest-sse-subscribe` COMPLETE. The atom's grade was standing on a red witness.

THE CAUSE IS THAT DELIVERY WAS OPTIONAL. R2703's buffered subscription stages a sample in the callback -- correct, because the callback runs on the drive loop and cannot wait -- and moves it to the consumer in `Session::drain_buffered`, which a host must wire as `LoopStages::after_dispatch`. `drive_session_until_terminal`, the simple entry point that 142 call sites use, defaults that stage to `|| core::future::ready(())`. So a subscription declared through it answered healthily and delivered nothing. The differential leg drives exactly that way; the local SSE leg wires the stage, which is why one was green and the other red, and why nothing local caught it.

THE REPAIR MAKES THE COMMON CASE NOT NEED THE HOST. The callback now sends directly when the stage is empty and the consumer has room, and stages only when it does not -- so a full channel still moves its wait off the loop, which is what the seam was built for. Ordering is preserved by construction: the direct send is taken only under the stage lock and only when nothing is staged, and the drain now reserves a channel permit BEFORE popping, then pops and sends under one hold of that lock.

That permit also closes a defect nobody had named: `park_on_drain` races the drain in a `select!`, and the previous shape popped an item and then awaited its send, so a cancelled park DROPPED that sample. A future cancelled while awaiting a permit has taken nothing out of the stage.

Two debt items, and the interesting half of each is what the measurement REFUSED.

ITEM 783 ASKED FOR A TYPE OR A GATE, and its own body prescribed something stronger first: make the simple drive entry wire the buffered drain itself, so delivery under backpressure stops depending on the host. That prescription came with a warning to MEASURE the cost rather than estimate it, and the measurement killed it. `drive_session_until_terminal` does not take a `Session` -- its arguments are the driver, the link actions, the engine, a clock, timeouts and an event closure -- so the loop cannot see the buffered registry at all. The one route from the loop to the session is `on_event`, and that is SYNCHRONOUS, so it cannot await a drain. Putting the registry where the loop does look means `SessionCore`, and `wz-session-core` carries ZERO boxed futures today; the drain is an `async fn` in all but name, so that move would introduce executor shape into a `no_std` kernel the MCU profiles link.

⇒ "delivery works with no host stage" is an ARCHITECTURE change and it needs to be its own item, not a clause inside this one. What the title asked for -- that the invariant be held by something other than a `log::error!` -- does not need it.

SO THE OBLIGATION BECAME A VALUE. `declare_subscriber_buffered` now returns a third thing, a `#[must_use]` `BufferedDrainStage`, which this workspace's `-D warnings` turns into a build error for a caller that drops it. The second line is a gate over the derived population of call sites, whose selftest drives a wired crate, an unwired one, a DISCARDED one, and an empty population -- that last because a scan that finds no caller has lost its subject rather than passed.

ITEM 784 ASKED FOR A MEASUREMENT AND THE ANSWER IS THE GOOD ONE. Round 2708.decision_summary:
The owner asked for the long-term-correct fix with cost ignored, and the interesting part is that the expensive candidates were all wrong and the tree already owned the right shape.

THE INVARIANT, STATED PLAINLY. A buffered subscription applies backpressure by making the drive loop WAIT, because waiting is what stops the loop reading the link, which is what closes the peer's window. So the loop must be able to learn that it owes a wait. Until now the only route to that knowledge was `LoopStages::after_dispatch`, supplied by the host — and `drive_session_until_terminal`, the entry 289 of 308 call sites use, defaults it to a no-op.

R2707 could only make forgetting LOUD, and its own register entry said why in advance: measure before estimating. The measurement was that the loop does not take a `Session` at all (`driver`, `actions`, `engine`, `clock`, `timeouts`, `on_event`), and its one route to one — `on_event` — is SYNCHRONOUS, so it cannot await anything.

THE THREE CANDIDATES I HAD WRITTEN DOWN WERE ALL WORSE THAN THE ONE I HAD NOT. ⑴ move the registry into `SessionCore` — but that crate carries ZERO boxed futures and the lwIP MCU profile, which has no executor, links it. ⑵ a new entry that takes the session — leaves "the host chooses" intact, which is R2707 again. ⑶ delete the channel and have the consumer pull from the stage — plausible, and still a redesign of the delivery path.

THE FOURTH IS THE TREE'S OWN IDIOM. `SessionRuntime` already abstracts what differs per profile and never looks inside: `LinkSink`, `Shared<U>`, `ActionsHandle`. Adding `IterationWork` to it puts the session's per-iteration work exactly where `SessionLinkActions::core` already lives — the one thing the loop holds that means "this session" — while the kernel's whole interaction with the value stays `Default::default()`. The tokio profile binds the buffered registry, because an async drain is the RUNTIME's vocabulary; the MCU profile binds `()` and pays a zero-sized field. No future entered `no_std`, which was ⑴'s only objection, and no call site of the 289 moved.

⚠ THE COMPILER MADE THE PUBLIC SURFACE SMALLER THAN I FIRST WROTE IT. A generic `Session<R, ..>` needs two things of that work, so a trait carries them — and both are SYNCHRONOUS (`register`, `stage`). `register` takes an opaque `RegisteredDrain` rather than the `dyn BufferedDrain` I reached for first, because Rust refused to expose a private trait through a public one. The refusal was right: what a drain IS stays this crate's business, and the awaiting is done by the loop, which knows the concrete type.

AND THE HALF THAT IS A REMOVAL. R2707's `#[must_use]` said "drop this and your subscription stalls". That was true when written and is FALSE now, so it is gone; a lint stating a consequence that no longer follows teaches a reader something untrue about the code it sits on. Its gate is gone too, and it proved its own subject had vanished: this round's witness drives the ordinary entry and discards the handle on purpose, which is exactly the shape that gate refused. A check that refuses correct code is worse than no check.

THE CLAUSE IMPLIES ONE ABSENCE AND THE MEASUREMENT FOUND TWO. Item 761's (b) reads "a second binding kind (`lifecycle:`) in `wz-switchboard.yaml`, so the AP registry and the MCU's generated static match take their row from the SAME document". Taken literally that is a schema field. Measured:

(1) THE DOCUMENT COULD NOT EXPRESS THE ROW, for a reason deeper than a missing field. `SwitchboardSpec` derives a row's kind from `Binding::codec` PRESENCE -- a two-valued discriminator with no room for a third state -- and its unit is ONE machine, cross-checked by the generator against that machine's `external_ingress_events`. A close verb belongs to the SESSION FSM, which every profile already has and which no sidecar names. So a lifecycle row in `bindings` would ask the generator to validate a session event against an application machine, where it correctly does not exist.

(2) THERE WAS NO AP RENDERER AT ALL. `grep -rln SwitchboardSpec --include=*.rs crates/` returns exactly two files: the schema and the MCU generator. `wz-switchboard-example` populated a registry with three literal `register*` calls under a comment reading "the SAME routing as wz-switchboard.yaml … in production the AP loader fills this by parsing the runtime sidecar". There was no such loader. The comment had been asserting a component into existence, which is this tree's "an asserted binding is not a binding" in its plainest form -- and the schema crate's own module doc said the same thing more honestly, calling the AP seam "a future" one.

WHAT WAS BUILT, and each choice is forced rather than picked. `SwitchboardSpec::lifecycle` is a SECOND SECTION, not a third flavour of `Binding`, because what differs between the sections is not payload shape but WHICH MACHINE the row targets. `LifecycleBinding` carries keyexpr + event and has no `codec` field at all, so "a codec on a lifecycle row" is unrepresentable rather than forbidden by a rule nobody runs -- a command's subject travels in its keyexpr by the owner's own grammar decision.

`SwitchboardRegistry::apply_spec` is the mapping, and it lives ON THE REGISTRY beside `register` / `register_value` / `register_command`. That placement is the repair, not a convenience: the defect is hosts writing their own rows, so the cure has to sit where a host is already looking. A separate loader crate would have been one hop away and easy not to find. A TTY LISTENER CAN NOW TELL "MY PEER IS STILL HERE" FROM "MY PEER IS GONE", AND EVERY SERIAL LISTENER DEFECT ABOVE THAT WAS A CONSEQUENCE OF ITS NOT BEING ABLE TO.

⛔ THE BASE WAS AN ABSENCE, NOT A WRONG VALUE. `SerialListener` carried a one-shot `armed: bool`: cleared by the first accept, so every later accept parked. That was the honest model while it was the only one available — wz's accept seam has no link-liveness feedback, and the two behaviours a listener must distinguish are indistinguishable without it. But "one link at a time" and "one link ever" are different rules, and the code could only express the second. Upstream expresses the first with an `is_connected: Arc<AtomicBool>` shared between the link and the accept task (`io/zenoh-links/zenoh-link-serial/src/unicast.rs` @ `while is_connected.load(Ordering::Acquire) {`, stored true at @ `is_connected.store(true, Ordering::Release);` and cleared by the link's own close at @ `self.is_connected.store(false, Ordering::Release);`), so its tty listener serves peer after peer.

WHAT WAS BUILT IS THAT FEEDBACK, in the shape wz's teardown actually has. `SerialLiveness` is the shared flag; `SerialLiveness::claim` is the only way to set it and it RETURNS the guard that clears it, so a claim cannot be taken without taking the thing that releases it. The release rides `Drop` rather than a `close` method because wz's accepted link has no close call of its own -- it is torn down by being dropped, and a teardown step that must be REMEMBERED is the class this workspace files against itself.

THE GUARD REACHES THE LINK THROUGH A NEWTYPE, WHICH IS WHY THE DIFF IS SMALL. `SerialPort` is a `SerialStream` plus an OPTIONAL guard, and it takes the place of the bare stream in `DialedLink::Serial`/`AcceptedLink::Serial` under the SAME field name. The option is not laxity: a DIAL owns its device outright and reports to nobody, an ACCEPT borrows it from a listener that will hand it out again, and that is a real difference between the two ways to get a serial link. The production lib compiled on the first attempt; every error was a hand-composed link in a test.

⚠ `release_on_close` IS REFUSED, NOT HONOURED, AND THAT IS THIS ROUND'S HONEST HALF RATHER THAN A SHORTFALL HIDDEN IN A DEFAULT. Reshaping a workspace-wide contract for one scheme would be the wrong base. Round 2727.decision_summary:
`transport-link-serial` grades COMPLETE: its last residual clause,
`release_on_close`, is built, and REMAINING WORK falls 25 -> 24.

The base fixed was a MISSING ROUTE, not a wrong value. R2704 was right
that honouring the key could not be a serial-side patch: wz's accept
MOVES the stream into the link, `tokio::io::split` then puts the two
halves in different owners -- the READ half in `SerialReadDriver`, which
the session drops at teardown, and the WRITE half inside a spawned
writer task whose contract is `Output = ()` across ten pipelines -- so a
dying link had nowhere to give the device BACK to. That route is now
`SerialRetainSlot`, inside the `SerialLiveness` the listener already
shares with its link: the one object both halves can reach. The writer
task contract is untouched, because the task takes the channel as an
ARGUMENT and returns its half through it.

The rule is both halves or neither. `unsplit` panics on halves that are
not a pair, so the device is retained only when both arrive and the next
accept re-opens otherwise. That is DERIVED from `WriterHandle`'s three
exits rather than chosen: `drain` and dropping the handle end the task
normally and return the half, while `abort` cancels it mid-await and the
half goes with it -- and that call's own doc names its use, "callers
tearing down a session whose link is already gone". A tty whose writer
was cancelled mid-frame is in an unknown state, so re-opening is right
there. The divergence is stated rather than hidden: upstream keeps the
port however the link died, so `release_on_close=false` is a BEST-EFFORT
retain in wz.

changes_bullets: `ChainStaging` gains a PAIR, `buf(chain, want)` and `commit(chain, filled)`, and
both arenas implement it. `buf` lends a writable slice a filler writes in place;
`commit` stages what the filler reports and discards the rest of the
reservation.
THE PAIR IS NOT AN ORNAMENT, and the round found that out by trying to write the
witness rather than by reasoning about it. A first cut put only `buf` on the
trait, and it was wrong twice over. The heap arm has to MATERIALISE a
reservation to lend a `&mut [u8]`, so its length moved while the pooled arm's
did not -- two implementations of one trait, observably different. And a socket
read returns fewer bytes than its buffer whenever the peer sent fewer, which is
the ordinary case, so a `buf` that staged its own reservation would stage bytes
nobody wrote. Each chain now carries the outstanding reservation: the pooled arm
advances a length it never moved, the heap arm gives back the tail it had to
materialise, and the two are observationally identical.
`BoundedVec<u8, N>` gains `grow_for_fill` and `truncate` to support the heap
arm. `grow_for_fill` takes a LENGTH rather than returning the declared capacity,
and that is forced by the type's own documented contract -- "a live one costs
what it actually staged" -- which a `CAP`-wide slice would break by zero-filling
to `CAP`. Both cfg arms are written: `N` is advisory on the `alloc` backing and
a hard limit on the no-alloc one, exactly as `push` already documents.

the chain through its own private method, so this type had two ways to move one
fact. `read_fixed_into` takes its destination from `buf` and resolves it with

than done silently.

writes where the chain already is. The second drives a SHORT fill across BOTH
arenas in one test, because they resolve it by opposite mechanics and the claim
is that those agree -- two separate tests could each pass while the arenas
disagreed. The third fixes that `commit` refuses more than was lent, on both.

Round 2737.decision_summary:
R2736 established that the AP profile has NO LINK-RX POOL: `out/wz-runtime-tokio`
holds one emit, `reassembly_pool_ap.rs`, while the MCU side has
`session_rx_pool_mcu`, `session_rx_pool_mcu_multicast` and `scout_rx_pool_mcu`
BESIDE `reassembly_pool_mcu`. This round did not declare that pool, and the
reason is the ordering rather than the work.

A pool declared this round would have had NO CONSUMER until the next one, and
this module's own history says what that costs: `zero_copy.rs` records that the
generated pools were read "for their CONSTANTS only", that "the seven-state
lifecycle FSM had zero callers", and that `runtime-zero-copy` was therefore "a
Cargo.toml flag that toggled nothing". Adding a second inert emit to fix the
first would repeat the defect while appearing to work on it.

So the order is: make the seam shareable FIRST, where consumers already exist,

"new pool" was wrong twice over before this round measured it.

IT ALREADY EXISTED AS A DECLARATION. `deploy/ap_mcu_pair.yaml`'s
`ap_node.buffer_pools.session_rx_pool` carried `{ slot_count: 64, slot_size:
4096, ... }` inline, with no scxml and no emit, so nothing could consume it and
nothing graded it. The same file's note above the MCU block says why those moved
out: dims "live ONLY in their scxml SSOTs ... values NOT duplicated". The AP one
was that migration, still pending. So this is a MIGRATION AND A CORRECTION, not
a greenfield add.

AND THE DECLARED SIZE COULD NOT HOLD ONE BATCH. The same node declares
`qos.batch_size: 65536` beside a 4096-byte slot -- sixteen times too small. That
is the defect `reassembly_pool_ap.scxml` records in its own comment, in the
other direction: a pool dimension taken from something that is not what the link
delivers. There it was the 1472-byte link mtu, which left the TCP reassembly
window ONE BYTE wide and made `transport-fragmentation` unobservable end to end.

SO THE SIZE WAS READ OFF THE RECEIVE PATH, not off a deploy number. The stream
reader refuses a prefix whose `payload_len` exceeds `u16::MAX`, then sizes its
buffer `w + payload_len` where `w` is 2 universal / 4 lowlatency, and it keeps
the prefix IN the frame so the codec sees the wire bytes verbatim. The ceiling
is therefore 4 + 65535 = 65539, and 65536 -- the value that looks right -- is
THREE BYTES SHORT on the lowlatency arm. Rounded to this node's 64-byte
alignment: 65600.

omission. A slot count here is not a correctness bound: `RxSlots::reserve`
returns `None` when the pool is dry and its contract calls that back-pressure
rather than an error, so the number trades throughput against residency and does
not decide whether a frame can be received. It needed no re-derivation to be
correct, so it was left alone.

production link's bytes still landed somewhere the pool had never heard of and

THE SHAPE IS UPSTREAM'S, READ AND NOT INVENTED. The pinned zenoh's registered
buffers are an OWNED handle over borrowed storage -- `RxBuffer { data: &'static
mut [u8], buf_id: u16, arena: Arc<ReservableArenaInner> }` with a Drop that
recycles the id (`commons/zenoh-uring/src/linux/api/reader/rx_buffer.rs` @ `impl Drop for RxBuffer {`), whose

and the Arc it goes home to. It is NOT a borrow, for the same reason
`RecycledBuf` is not one -- a lifetime would tie every frame to a borrow of the
arena, and `poll_framed` holds its frame across an await inside a `ReadState`
its driver owns beside that arena.

non-uring pool is per LINK because it is one mtu-sized buffer at the pinned
defaults; this one is 64 x 65600 = about 4.2 MiB and `deploy/ap_mcu_pair.yaml`
declares it once per NODE. Sixty-four slots serve sixty-four links, because a
read half holds at most one frame at a time -- so per-link tables would
multiply the memory by the link count to buy nothing. `LinkRxArena::node()` is
a handle on one process-wide table; `LinkRxArena::new()` builds a private one,
and that second constructor is not a test affordance but the seam a later round
threads a node object into, which is why the witnesses use it.

Build the structure `runtime-tokio-uring`'s first residual actually needs:
frame boundaries over bytes the reader did not size.

merely unbuilt, it was inexpressible. This round builds that type and the read
that feeds it; nothing yet SELECTS the path, which is the half of the residual
that remains and is now a task rather than a structure that does not exist.

Round 2755.decision_summary:
A type that takes a process-global, kernel-accounted charge must give it
back on the schedule it took it. `FixedSlotRing::register` pins
`SLOT_COUNT * SLOT_SIZE` bytes against `RLIMIT_MEMLOCK` and, until this
round, had no release of its own: the charge came back when the kernel
finished tearing the ring's context down after its fd closed, which
`io_uring` does on a workqueue. Everything built on top of that absence
was compensation for it — Layer C1br serializes the registering tests,
`register_awaiting_reclaim` sleeps up to 500ms for the kernel, and
`uring-memlock.sh` raises the ceiling until the leak stops mattering.
`impl Drop for FixedSlotRing` unregisters inside the drop; the
compensations stay, and each now covers only the case it always named
and could not reach — a ceiling contended by another PROCESS.

Second decision, in the instrument rather than the subject. A guard must
ask the question its body exists to answer. `uring_raise_memlock`'s
privileged raise was gated on `(( soft < need ))`, where `need` is one
registration's worth, while the body under it explains at length that it
asks for `unlimited` because a binary registering in several tests holds
earlier charges. On a host whose ceiling admits one registration and not
two the guard is false and the body never runs. The guard now asks
whether this process may have more at all, which is yes whenever the
ceiling is not already unlimited.

Third, and it is the same rule applied to two more places in that file:
the page-headroom formula rounded the pool's byte TOTAL when the kernel
charges per REGION, and the capability probe registered ONCE when every
caller runs a binary that registers per test. A probe that measures a
capability the lane does not exercise reports ready for something else.

Fourth, uncovered by the first three and paid here rather than deferred
because it shares the seam: `UringReactor::attach` took a prefix WIDTH
and froze it for the link's life. The justification cited
`crate::poll_framed`'s rule, which fixes the width at frame START —
once per frame, not once per link. The two premises behind the
generalisation are true and the conclusion is false: a link's first read
is its HANDSHAKE, which precedes the Established flip, so a link that
negotiated lowlatency kept the universal 2-byte prefix on a 4-byte wire.
`attach` now takes the link's own flag and the worker re-derives the
width where `RxWindow::between_frames()` already says it may.

What is NOT decided here, stated so it is not read as covered: a single
completion carrying the last universal frame and the first lean one is
read at one width. Upstream avoids that by dispatching to the ring only
after the transport is established; wz dispatches at first poll. The
residual is recorded in `attach`'s own doc and in the witness, which is
written so the boundary is explicit rather than hidden.

A ratchet whose POPULATION is derived cannot report a rise as a
violation by the commit that caused the rise, because the two are
routinely different commits — and in this case the causing commit did
nothing wrong at all.

`upstream_citation_anchor_gate`'s root-less axis derives its candidate
segments from the directory components of the tree's own ROOTED
citations. That derivation is right and is what open-debt 647 bought:
a hand-listed population would grade one segment and miss fifty. What
comes with it is that writing ONE correctly-rooted citation in a
directory nothing had rooted before teaches the axis a new segment, and
every pre-existing root-less token under that segment is counted at
once, in files the commit never opened.

So this round's decision is to pay the content and register the form.
The twenty newly-visible citations get their roots, which is the repair
the gate asks for and is independently correct — six of them turned out
to name a path the pin does not have. The gate's REFUSAL TEXT is what

▶ AN OUTCOME THE CALLER CANNOT NAME IS ONE NOBODY CAN ACT ON. The first
version of this bound just `continue`d. Giving the refusal its own
`AcceptEvent` variant — rather than folding it into `FaceUp` or
`FaceFailed`, both of which would have been false — is what made it
observable to an operator AND made the witness expressible without a
timer. A non-`#[non_exhaustive]` enum then forces every consumer to
decide, which is the point rather than a cost.
▶ NEXT, AND IT IS THE LAST CLAUSE OF THIS ATOM: acceptor statelessness.
wz's cookie is a 16-byte `HMAC-SHA256(key, nonce ‖ peer_zid)` tag;
upstream's CARRIES the negotiated state and is round-tripped through
InitAck/OpenSyn, which is what lets its acceptor hold nothing between
them. So the work is changing what the cookie IS — serialising the
accept-state into it — not moving a check. The cookie is opaque to the
peer (it echoes it verbatim), so the encoding is wz's to choose and the
change is interop-safe.
⚠ AND THE SAME SEAM OWNS THE DIVERGENCE THIS ROUND LEFT: wz refuses
after a full handshake because its open is atomic. Staging the open is
what would let the bound refuse earlier AND let the acceptor hold
nothing — one change, two clauses. Worth weighing before treating them
as independent.
changes_bullets: `transport/unicast/max_sessions` now flows parsed config -> `WzConfig`

accept_loop}.rs` carry the six touchpoints `max_links` already had

THE FIELD IS UNGATED, unlike the `max_links` beside it. Aggregation is a
`transport-multilink` capability; a bound on how many peers a node
carries is a property of every build. That costs 16 construction sites,
which is the price of the property rather than a reason to avoid it.
Existing sites take `usize::MAX` — a test that does not exercise the
bound must not silently acquire it, or its subject changes underneath
it.
`accept_loop`'s own internal `FaceSources` takes
`config::DEFAULT_MAX_SESSIONS`, NOT `usize::MAX`. That entry carries no
configuration of its own, and the honest reading of that is upstream's
shipped value rather than the absence of a bound: zenoh has no unbounded
mode. The constant lives in `config.rs` because `accept_loop` is
feature-gated and this default is not — a constant that disappears with
a feature cannot be a config layer's default.

the two it is not are the argument. `FaceUp` is false — the face never
entered the table. `FaceFailed` is false too, and more interestingly:
that variant means "never reached Established", while this face
completed the whole handshake and was turned away after it. Folding it
into either would make a caller's count of opens or of handshake
failures wrong. `wz-ap-demo` logs it at WARN, not info: unlike an accept
error, a node at its bound does not clear by itself.

A node must bound how many peers it will hold, and the bound belongs at
the moment the table is added to — not after.

`session-unicast-accept` carries three residual clauses, and this round
began by re-measuring all three rather than acting on them, because the
entry says of itself "STILL OPEN in this entry and NOT re-measured".
That self-flag turned out to be an instruction: one of the three was
already false.

* `initial_sn is static rather than Shake128-derived from the zid pair`
  is REFUTED. Upstream's premise holds —
  `io/zenoh-transport/src/unicast/establishment/mod.rs` @
  `pub(super) fn compute_sn` is
  `Shake128(zid1 ‖ zid2)` masked by the frame-SN resolution, and the
  code states why: multilink needs the same `initial_sn` per attempt
  without storing state. But wz HAS that, in
  `wz-session-core/src/initial_sn.rs` @ `derive_initial_sn`, and the
  ACCEPTOR uses it. The witness is `session_glue`'s
  `openack_announces_the_derived_origin_not_zero`, whose own comment
  anticipates the alleged defect — "a fix wired only into the initiator
  would leave every wz acceptor on the constant" — and excludes the old
  value by name, `assert_ne!(announced, 0, "the pre-R311y816 constant
  origin")`. The clause has been dead since R311y816.
* `there is no max_sessions bound` is TRUE, and is what this round
  builds.
* `the acceptor is not stateless` is TRUE and is NOT this round's. It is
  a different kind of change: upstream's cookie CARRIES the negotiated
  state (zid, whatami, resolution, batch_size, nonce, per-extension
  `StateAccept`), while wz's is a 16-byte
  `HMAC-SHA256(key, nonce ‖ peer_zid)` tag. Making the acceptor
  stateless means changing what the cookie IS, not where it is checked.

The bound goes where upstream puts it.
`io/zenoh-transport/src/unicast/manager.rs` @ `max_sessions` denies
under the session-table guard, immediately after its connection-to-self
check, returning `close::reason::INVALID`. wz's accept loop holds
that table as `faces`, and its dedup-by-zid rule is the analogue of the
self/dup check — so the comparison sits directly under that rule and
BEFORE `faces.insert`, because a bound applied after admission is not a
bound.

⚠ THE DIVERGENCE THAT REMAINS, stated rather than discovered later: wz
refuses AFTER the handshake completes, because its accept path opens a
face in one step where upstream's establishment is staged. Upstream
spends an InitSyn on a peer it will refuse; wz spends the whole 4-way.
The peer also learns less — it sees its link close rather than a close
reason. Neither is fixed here; both are properties of where wz's open
becomes atomic, which is the same seam the statelessness clause names.

not asserted — both dial the same loopback listener and the accept order

changes_bullets: `crates/wz-session-core/src/accept_cookie.rs` is new, `alloc`-gated
beside `signing_key` for its reason — the cookie is a `Vec<u8>`
authenticated by that module's key, so the two share a footing.
`AcceptCookieState` carries `peer_zid` (1..=16), `peer_whatami`,
`sn_res`, `batch_size`, `nonce`, and the four negotiated outcomes
(`lowlatency`, `qos`, `compression`, `shm`) as a bitset. Wire layout:
`nonce(8) ‖ whatami(1) ‖ sn_res(1) ‖ batch_size(2) ‖ flags(1) ‖
zid_len(1) ‖ zid ‖ tag(16)`, little-endian like every other wz integer.
Widest form is 46 bytes.
`encode_accept_cookie` returns `Option`, refusing a zid outside the
protocol's 1..=16 rather than minting a cookie for a zid the wire cannot
carry. `decode_accept_cookie` VERIFIES BEFORE IT PARSES and returns a
two-variant error: `Tampered` when the tag fails, `Malformed` when it
verified and the payload still did not parse. Collapsing them would lose
the only actionable distinction — a bad tag is an attacker or a rotated
key, a bad length is this code disagreeing with itself — and because the
tag is checked first, `Malformed` is only ever reached for bytes this
key actually signed.
`signing_key` gains `cookie_payload_tag` and
`cookie_payload_tag_verify`. The verifier is `hmac`'s
`verify_truncated_left`, not a slice `==`: the cookie is handed to an
unauthenticated peer by construction, so a short-circuiting compare
leaks the expected tag a byte at a time to anyone willing to retry.
The tag covers the WHOLE payload, where the tag-only form covered the
zid. Every field here is state the acceptor will act on, so each one is
under the MAC or the peer chooses it.
Round 2760.decision_summary:
The structure that makes wz's acceptor stateful is not where a check
happens. It is what the cookie IS.

`session-unicast-accept`'s last residual reads "the acceptor is not
stateless". zenoh's acceptor holds nothing between InitAck and OpenSyn
because its cookie CARRIES the negotiated state —
`io/zenoh-transport/src/unicast/establishment/cookie.rs` @
`pub(crate) struct Cookie` is zid, whatami, resolution, batch_size,
nonce and a `StateAccept` per extension, minted into InitAck and
returned in OpenSyn. wz's cookie is
`HMAC-SHA256(cookie_signing_key, nonce ‖ peer_zid)[..16]`: a sixteen-byte
TAG. It proves the peer echoed something bound to its zid and it can
carry nothing, so wz must remember instead — which it does, in a
`SessionActions` built before InitSyn and held through the handshake.

So this round builds the carrier. `crates/wz-session-core/
src/accept_cookie.rs` is a cookie that carries the acceptor's whole
InitSyn-derived state under a MAC.

⚠ THE PAYLOAD IS DERIVED FROM WZ, NOT COPIED FROM UPSTREAM, and the two
agreeing is the finding rather than the method. `SessionLinkActions`'s
`is_ack: false` arm populates exactly four slots, every one a pure
function of the InitSyn body: `inbound_peer_zid` and `remote_peer_zid`
(both `body.zid`), `peer_whatami`, and `inbound_peer_init_caps`
(`sn_res`, `batch_size`). The extension half is a handful of bools,
because a peer's offers reach the acceptor only through
`negotiate_lowlatency_against_peer(peer_offered: bool)` and its qos /
compression / shm siblings. That is upstream's `StateAccept` shape,
arrived at independently.

⚠⚠ AND THE EXTENSION CHAIN IS NOT PART OF IT, which is what makes the
design fit at all. The `init_syn_ext` / `init_ack_ext` / `open_syn_ext`
/ `open_ack_ext` slots read like stores of what arrived. They are not:
all eight of their consumers are SEND-side, and `init_syn_ext` is
initialised to a local `default_init_patch_ext_entry()`. Had the raw
chain needed carrying it would not have fit — `ExtEntry`'s own
`MAX_ENCODED_BYTES` is 42 against a generated cookie field of
`Option<S::Bytes<128>>`, a cap that is advisory on the Heap storage
profile and HARD on the no-alloc Inline one.

THE KEY DOES NOT LEAVE ITS MODULE. `SigningKey::as_slice` is private and
its own doc states the boundary — "only this module's
`generate_cookie_hmac_sha256` can read them". Widening it to
`pub(crate)` would have been one word. Instead `signing_key` lends two
OPERATIONS, `cookie_payload_tag` and `cookie_payload_tag_verify`, and
the bytes stay where they were. The smaller edit was the weaker type.

WHAT THIS ROUND DOES NOT DO, so the next one is not misled: nothing
stages the handshake and nothing replays an InitSyn. The acceptor still
builds its engine before InitSyn and holds it, and no wire byte changes.
The carrier comes first because the staging cannot be written until
there is something for the peer to hand back.

star's first clause — a standing CI red comes first — and both of its causes

What the next round should know, worked out here and not obvious from the

THE BASE FOR `session-unicast-accept` IS NOT MORE COOKIE FIELDS. Upstream's
acceptor is not stateless: it keeps ONE u64 across the boundary and rebuilds
everything else from the cookie, refusing a replay by comparing the returned
nonce against the one it kept. That keeps the existing discriminator test
`a_cookie_from_an_earlier_handshake_is_refused_by_the_next` CORRECT — a fully
stateless design would have had to break it, and breaking it would have been
justified as the price of statelessness.
The population of what the cookie must carry was derived wrongly in R2760 and
is corrected here. It is NOT the four slots the `is_ack: false` arm fills; it
is what the establishment demux writes on an admitted Init, and the comment at
`crates/wz-session-core/src/session_actions.rs` @ `establishment demux` says
so itself. That set is nine, and three of its members are not booleans. Independently, upstream's cookie field list
matches it one-to-one, which is the cross-check: two derivations, one answer.
So R2760's carrier is the scalar half, and its module doc claiming `the
acceptor's WHOLE InitSyn-derived state` overclaims and must be corrected.
The structure that does NOT exist here is a per-extension accept-state seam.
Upstream gives TEN establishment extensions their own state type and codec
pair, and its cookie is a struct over them; this tree spells that type in
seventeen prose citations and implements it zero times. The auth half proves
the difference is reach rather than size: the acceptor's usrpwd challenge
lives inside a boxed trait object whose trait has no way to export or reinject
it, so no amount of cookie capacity gets at it. The dividing line for that
seam is peer-derived state travels, node-local capability is rebuilt from
config — upstream draws the same line.
That seam must NOT be invented. `SceSink` and `SceCursor` already are it: a
fixed sink raises a buffer-overflow error where a growable one returns
success, which is how the generated codecs serve both storage profiles from
one body of code. Building on them also removes the `alloc` gate that
currently makes the cookie module absent on the no-alloc profile — the same
profile where the 128-byte cookie capacity is hard rather than advisory. The
budget was measured and is not the constraint: roughly 101 bytes of 128.
ONE DEBT IS REGISTERED BY DESCRIPTION HERE AND NOT YET BY NUMBER. Any
untracked file in the worktree still makes the runner decline, so every push
stops until someone reads the runner's lines. Gate 3 now names that honestly,
which is the repairable half; the half that remains is that the condition
itself is easy to create and its cost is a whole push cycle. The population
for a proper registration was not derived, and filing without deriving it is
the failure this repository has a rule against.

Pay the standing hosted red at its base, and fix what made the payment
expensive rather than only what made it fail.

The round opened with gate 2c refusing a push over run 35510863717. Both of
that run's failing jobs carried ONE cause: `scripts/lib/uring-memlock.sh` @

owns, and the probe's embedded python DEFINES the opcode it issues, so the
comment can name a symbol its own file carries. A name that can be grepped in

than because they were cheap.

red cargo arrives as 101. The base is therefore INSIDE this repository — the
hook throwing away a distinction its runner already provides — and not
upstream, so it is fixed here rather than registered and asked about.

SECOND — the hosted verdict moved while the round ran. Asking the gate's own
instrument rather than reusing the ack id showed it now grades 35515719160,

make the nonce per-handshake and the acceptor has something to check, put the
negotiated state on the cookie and it has nothing else to hold.

NEITHER seam could have drawn again -- the AP one named its source inline
and the MCU one took a borrow that ends when the function returns. The
defect is therefore not the draw site. It is that the bundle held a VALUE
where a per-handshake secret needs a SOURCE with the bundle's lifetime.

by both production construction seams, and a draw inside the InitAck path --
the same place zenoh draws. The MCU seam's signature changed from a borrow
to ownership for exactly this reason, which is the change that makes the
design expressible rather than a consequence of it.

A consumer of the capture surface asked for a `zid` term in the selector
language: it wants to filter records by the node that sent them, and had
no way to. The term was the visible half. The half that decides whether
a term can mean anything is whether a `RecordView` reaches the predicate
with an identity on it at all, and it did not — the struct carried nine
fields and none of them named a node. Adding the word alone would have
given the grammar a term with nothing to evaluate.

DECIDED — the identity comes FROM THE NODE PLANE and is not read a
second time. `crate::payload` already states this rule for `kind`:
deriving it locally is "the second spelling that would let the two
planes disagree about one record". A walk that recognised nodes for
itself would be exactly that, one plane over.

DECIDED — the carrier is the grouping that was ALREADY going there.
`SessionGrouping` is keyed by list index, holds two entries in
`Direction` order, documents that alignment where it is built, and is
handed to all three record walks. What it did not keep was the identity:
`SpaceOwner::Session` interns `(session, node)` into a token that cannot
be inverted, and `session_grouping` builds its census and drops it. So
the repair is not new plumbing, it is declining to throw away something
already derived. The alternative — a second census inside the walks —
would have been the second spelling above.

DECIDED — an unnamed sender is UNDECIDABLE, not rejected, and its
negation is undecidable too. A link exists only where both ends sent an
INIT on one flow, so a capture that began mid-session has no link for
its lists. Those records still HAVE a sender; this capture never saw it
name itself. Answering `no` would put "could not tell" and "was someone
else" in one bucket, and a reader asking `zid == x` would read a silent
drop as a measured exclusion. The negation rides inside the term for the
same reason: negating an unknown gives an unknown, and a record whose
sender cannot be named cannot be shown to be a different one either.

DECIDED — the written form is BARE HEX, and that is a measurement of the
consuming surface rather than a preference. Its row renderer already
prints a short byte field as exactly these characters, with no prefix
and no separators, so a reader can lift a zid off a row and drop it into

string it was written in, which is what makes the two cases of one zid
a single term instead of two that never match each other.

parameter would have made a caller that simply forgot indistinguishable

Round 2766.decision_summary:
A consumer of the capture surface has a census door that takes a selector
and a field door that emits rows, and nothing that does both. To show
"the messages matching this" it had one option left: take every row back
and apply the selector again on its own side. That is a second
implementation of this library's selector language living in the caller,
and two implementations of one language disagree eventually — in a place
neither side can debug from its own half.

DECIDED — the answer is not evaluated at render time. The naive shape is
to hang a selector on the fields door and judge there, and it is wrong
for a reason that is measurable rather than stylistic: that document is
produced by a different walk from the census one, so judging there would
build a SECOND `RecordView` per record. The record plane already builds
one and already asks the filter; the renderer consumes what that walk
decided.

DECIDED — the verdict is folded PER ROW, and that is the consumer's
decision rather than ours. A row may carry several records. Splitting a
row per record would need a coordinate for each, and a reassembled
record's span exists only inside a reader — so the split would force us
to invent coordinates, which is the failure this tree names most often.
Any match makes the row a match, all misses make it a miss, anything
else is undecided.

DECIDED — FOUR WORDS, not three and a null. `"yes"`, `"no"`,
`"undecided"` and `"unjudged"`, because the last two are different facts
that would otherwise render alike: one says the selector was applied and
this capture does not carry what deciding needs, the other says the row
holds nothing the record plane judges at all. A reader asking why a
filter missed something needs to know which, since only the first is
about the filter. The consumer draws the same line from its side for its
own half-rows, and a document that collapsed them would hand a gap back
as a measured exclusion.

DECIDED — the join key is `(list index, direction, message_at)`, and
each of the two obvious alternatives is wrong in a way that still
produces plausible numbers. `record_unit_offset` is a RECORD's offset
within its framing unit while the row carries a MESSAGE's offset within
its stream: they share one term and have different bases, so joining on
it points at the wrong place rather than failing. A flow key cannot
disambiguate two lists that share a 5-tuple, which this tree already
records as the reason a session grouping is keyed by list.

DECIDED — one renderer under both doors. The document without a selector
is the `None` case of the document with one, so the two cannot drift
into two programs a reader would have to compare.

Settle open-debt 801 by measurement, and the measurement refuted BOTH readings the item was registered with. The third cause is a vacuous fixture, not a product defect, so the item's own title was wrong. R2770 registered 801 as "the re-handshake's InitAck is not transmitted", with two candidate causes and an explicit note that neither had been measured. That flag's readers are `drive.rs`'s DATA path (`is_established() && transport_available`) and multilink's `select_link`; `emit_on_link` is a WRITER of it, closing it on `WriterGone`. Round 2772.decision_summary:
Close the half of session-unicast-accept's last clause that can be closed:
the acceptor now REBUILDS its negotiated state from the cookie the peer
echoed, where R2769 left the decoded copy being thrown away.

THE CLAUSE READS "the acceptor is not stateless because no negotiated ext
state rides the cookie". Its stated CAUSE is now false -- the state rides,
and the acceptor reads it back off the wire. Its HEADLINE is still true:
the slots are still held, and the rebuild writes INTO them rather than
replacing the holding. So the atom stays PARTIAL and REMAINING stays 21,
which is the honest grade rather than the flattering one.

THE SEAM WAS DERIVED, NOT CHOSEN. `drive.rs` computes `admit` (for
OpenSyn that is `cookie_valid()`), returns early on denial, and then runs
every per-frame negotiation merge. The rebuild goes in that admitted path,
so `cookie_valid` stays a PREDICATE. Upstream splits it the same way: the
nonce compare and `// Rebuild the state from the cookie` are both in
`recv_open_syn`, the handler. Installing state from a guard would put a
write inside a question.
⚠ AND IT GOES BEFORE THE OTHER MERGES, deliberately: those merge a peer's
OFFER off an Init frame, while this restores an OUTCOME already negotiated
in this handshake. A restore running after a merge would overwrite the
newer answer with the older.

⛔ THE DESIGN POINT THE ROUND TURNS ON, and it was MEASURED rather than
assumed. The obvious implementation installs through the `set_*_offer`
setters, whose slots are exactly the right ones. Enumerating all four
splits them 2/2: `set_lowlatency_offer` and `set_qos_offer` each REFUSE
while the other is on, `set_compression_offer` and `set_shm_offer` are
plain writes. So a setter-based rebuild is silently wrong for exactly two
of four -- the shape that passes any witness touching only the other two --
and because that pair is mutually exclusive it is not expressible in
EITHER call order. RESTORING AN OUTCOME IS NOT STAGING AN OFFER: those
setters carry staging policy because they run before negotiation, and the
value here has already been through it, so re-applying the policy applies
the rule twice. The restore writes the slots directly.

⚠ WHAT WAS NOT DONE, and the plan that said to do it was mine: R2769's
transitional `carried.peer_zid == peer_zid` check is KEPT. The carry said
to retire it, on the reasoning that once the rebuild installs from the
cookie the comparison is meaningless. That is false as written -- the
rebuild installs the five EXT STATES and does not touch the zid, so the
two copies can still disagree and the check is still live. It becomes
meaningless when the HELD zid goes, which is the separation round.
verification_bullets: CONTROLS, two arms, each restored byte-for-byte — and THE FIRST ATTEMPT AT
ARM A PROVED NOTHING: the damage did not compile, so its red was a build
error rather than a discrimination. Re-cut as a reachability change (match
`is_ack: true`, which an OpenSyn never is), both arms then COMPILED and
redded on exactly the new witness and nothing else:
A  the rebuild made unreachable -> the witness reds. It is load-bearing.
B  the patch restored through `negotiate_patch_against_peer` instead of a
direct write -> the witness reds. ⭐ THIS IS THE DESIGN CLAIM ITSELF rather
than a coverage check: that merge is a `min()` and cannot raise, so routing
a restore through a stager fails for the one member this build can observe.
The 2-of-4 setter split is therefore demonstrated, not argued.
WHY THE WITNESS CANNOT PASS BY ACCIDENT: it LOWERS the held level by hand —
the merge is monotonically non-increasing, so that disturbance is safe and
cannot be undone from inside the session — and then requires the level to
come back UP. A rise has no source but the cookie. That is the separation
between "the rebuild ran" and "the value was already right", which is where
a rebuild witness usually goes vacuous. An anti-vacuity guard fails the test
outright if the handshake negotiates a level too low to lower.

Keep this node's OFFER apart from what a link negotiated, and return the
negotiated slots to it at both handshake boundaries. That closes the half
of session-unicast-accept's last clause the five carried states cover, and
it fixes a reconnect defect with the same cause.

THE STEP THAT WAS PLANNED DID NOT HAVE A MEANING. The carry said "clear the
five carried slots after the mint". Reading what those slots hold before
writing the clear showed there was nothing to clear them TO: every
negotiated capability (is_qos, is_lowlatency, is_compression, is_shm, the
QoS band, the patch level) is seeded from an offer and then merged against
the peer IN ITS OWN SLOT. Once a link has negotiated, no slot says what was
offered. Clearing to false would have deleted the node's configuration.

THE SAME FUSION WAS A LIVE BUG, measured red-first before any fix.
`reset_for_reopen` left all six standing, so a reconnect negotiated from the
PREVIOUS LINK'S OUTCOME. Every merge moves one way (`&=`, `min()`, a band
that only narrows), so capability could only be lost across reconnects: a
flag once declined stayed declined, a patch once lowered stayed lowered,
and a QoS band once narrowed REFUSED any later acceptor answering outside
it. Upstream never has this: each link builds its state from the manager's
config.

THE FIX IS THE MISSING STRUCTURE, not the two call sites.
- `SessionCore.offer` holds a `SessionOffer`. The offer setters record into
  it; the merges write the slot only. `set_qos_link_metadata` was BOTH (the
  bring-up setter and the merge's writer) and is now only the former.
- The carried set is a TYPE, `NegotiatedExtensions`, with the codec. It was
  spelled four times (mint, encode, decode, rebuild); now the session writes
  its slots through ONE writer, `install_negotiated`, whether the value came
  off the wire or out of the offer.
- `return_to_offer` runs in `reset_for_reopen`: all six slots.
- After InitAck, ONLY when a carrying cookie went out, the five carried
  slots return to the offer; the OpenSyn rebuild puts the outcome back.
  Upstream's acceptor takes its State by value at InitAck and builds a new
  one from the cookie at OpenSyn.

Round 2775.decision_summary:
A consumer of the dissect doors confirmed, from a decision record of its own,
that it held a hand-kept copy of this library's ABI revision because the
header gave it no other shape. `wz_capi_c.h` has published its revision as a
macro beside the function since R2301; `wz_dissect.h` published it only as a
function. So a consumer of these doors could ask what it was RUNNING against
and never what it COMPILED against.

The consumer's argument went one layer below the stale literal, and that layer
is the reason this is a debt rather than a preference. Without the pair, the
dissect axis has NO means to detect a header describing a different library
than the one loaded -- and that failure is reachable wherever a prebuilt
library is handed in while the header comes from another checkout. A
hand-kept number and the loaded library can agree by coincidence while the
header describes a different contract, and nothing notices.

DECIDED -- take `wz_capi_c`'s shape exactly rather than invent a second one:
a Rust constant, the function returning it, the header macro, and the pin gate
reading both and refusing when they disagree.

DECIDED -- adding the macro does NOT move the revision. A define is compiled
in, not linked; the revision moves for a symbol or for the memory rule.

DECIDED -- this crate's own C consumer test stops holding a literal. It was the
fourth place the same number had to be moved by hand, every wrong move it
could catch is already refused by the gate, and the one thing the redundancy
bought was the stale copy that cost R2773 a hosted round. The deliberate-bump
forcing function stays in the gate's pin.

Round 2776.decision_summary:
Pay the Layer Q red R2774 left standing (hosted 35564799994,
Q.4.microbit.slim), at its base: the microbit deploys had no stack budget,
so their stacks overflowed into .bss in silence, and nothing measured how
close any of them was. Open-debt item 805.

THE RED WAS NOT R2774's ALONE, and the step's word "hang" was not the
cause. Measured with the memory map widened for measurement only, the
acceptor's peak stack was 7776 bytes BEFORE R2774 and 7920 after, against
7568 bytes its 16K layout left above .bss. The tree before R2774 was
already 208 bytes over and passing because what it overwrote was lwIP
state nothing on that path read; R2774's +144 reached `loop_netif` and the
boot faulted. So the fix is not "undo the +144". It is the structure whose
absence made a 208-byte overflow invisible.

THREE CHANGES, each at the place that generates its part:

1. THE STACK IS DECLARED, BELOW .data/.bss. The three microbit deploys
   (the acceptor, the qemu demo, the no-heap probe -- the whole population
   that boots on 16K) now give the stack its own linker region at the
   bottom of SRAM with a stated size. Past it the stack leaves SRAM and
   faults at the push that does it; a .bss that outgrows its share fails
   the link. The budgets are from measurement: acceptor 7K/9K, demo 3K/13K,
   probe 12K/4K.

2. THE PEAK IS MEASURED AND GATED. A new dependency-free crate,
   `wz-mcu-stack`, paints the region at entry and reads the deepest
   scrubbed word back; each deploy prints `stack: peak N of M bytes` and
   refuses PASS unless the peak stays 256 bytes (the footprint gate's own
   tolerance) under the budget. Layer Q keeps that line on PASS, so every
   run shows the margin, and fails a run of these deploys that exits 0
   WITHOUT it -- a binary that stopped measuring must not read as one that
   measured and fit. One crate, not three copies: the R311y21 reason
   `wz-mcu-clock` exists.

3. THE STACK IS PUT BACK INSIDE THE BUDGET, at the two places that
   generated the depth. (a) Every unicast action is `#[inline(never)]`:
   inlined into the engine's one dispatch frame, all actions shared a frame
   sized for the largest, so InitAck-only code raised the OpenAck path --
   exactly how R2774's +144 reached the peak. (b) `derive_initial_sn` no
   longer goes through `sha3::Shake128`, whose buffered wrapper took a
   1192-byte frame plus the permutation's 368 to hash at most 32 bytes on
   the acceptor's deepest path. The sponge is written over the same
   `keccak::f1600`, and `sha3::Shake128` -- what zenoh's `compute_sn` calls
   -- stays as the test oracle over every length pair and past the rate.

THE BOOL WAS NARROWER THAN THE NEGOTIATION. Under session-extqos wz merges

the accept loop reads the merged band after establishment. The cookie's
QoS state was a bool, so the band could neither ride it nor be released
after InitAck: releasing it would have lost the band the accept loop puts

THE SHAPE IS UPSTREAM'S, NOT A SECOND STATE BESIDE THE BOOL. Upstream's
qos accept state is one enum, `NoQoS | QoS { reliability, priorities }`,

pair and `Reliability`: `LinkPriorityRange` is gated on transport-qos and
`QosLinkState` on session-extqos, while the accept state module is
ungated so that its members are unconditional and only their values are.
The two conversions live beside the gated type.

`install_negotiated` writes the capability and the band from one value,
the InitAck release covers the band, and `return_to_offer` lost its

The auth challenges ride the accept cookie, and each method draws its own:
the first of the four states session-unicast-accept's stateless clause

because it is the same seam.

803 WAS REPRODUCED BEFORE IT WAS FIXED, through the production seams. A
responder built by `accept_and_open_session_with_auth` with usrpwd AND
pubkey, and an initiator whose two methods record what the InitAck handed
them, over loopback TCP: the test decrypts the pubkey challenge with the
initiator's own key and compares it to the usrpwd nonce the same InitAck
carried in the clear. On the unmodified tree they were byte-identical. The
register had recorded 803 from a code read only; this is the runtime probe
it said was missing.

THE BASE WAS THE FAN-OUT, NOT THE DRAW SITE. `AuthDispatch` offered one
setter, `set_challenge_nonce(u64)`, that handed one value to every method,
and the session exposed it as `refresh_auth_challenge_nonce`. Moving where
the seam called it would have kept the shape that made 803 expressible.
Both are gone: the dispatch takes one draw PER METHOD
(`set_drawn_challenges`), and the session draws them at InitAck from the
entropy source the bundle already carries for its cookie nonce -- the move
R2763 made for that nonce, to the place upstream draws (`prng.gen()` in
each method's accept path). The accept seam no longer draws at all; a
caller cannot reach an InitAck without passing the draw.

THE CARRY FOLLOWS UPSTREAM'S SHAPE. Upstream's auth accept state is one
optional u64 per configured method -- usrpwd's nonce, pubkey's challenge
(its codec writes nothing else). `AuthAcceptState` is exactly that, keyed
by method id, fixed width 18, placed after shm as upstream's cookie places
it, and it joins the one-writer group: the mint reads it after the auth
stage, the InitAck release writes "none" into both methods, and the OpenSyn
rebuild writes the carried values back before the auth stage checks against
them. A method outside upstream's two has no member and keeps its own
state, because releasing it would drop what nothing could return.

TWO ABSENCES HAD NO WAY TO BE SAID, and both are now Options. usrpwd's
nonce was a u64, so "no challenge outstanding" could only be whatever was
last in the slot. pubkey's OpenSyn stage skipped verification when no
initiator key had been captured -- harmless while the key was held, and a
skip of the whole check once the release drops it, which it must, since
upstream's pubkey state carries no key. Participation is now the restored
challenge, and its absence REFUSES at OpenSyn instead of skipping.

Round 2780.decision_summary:
The peer's announced region name rides the accept cookie: the second of the
four states session-unicast-accept's stateless clause names after R2777's
recount, the first being R2779's auth challenges.

THE SHAPE IS UPSTREAM'S STATE, NOT ITS BYTES. Upstream's region accept state
is one optional name (`other_region_name`), written into its cookie last,
after patch. wz carries exactly that, last, as `RegionAcceptState`: a length
and the name's bytes padded to upstream's longest name, width 33. It is not
held as the validated `RegionName` because the group is Copy and Eq and that
type is neither, which its own note records; the decode re-admits exactly
what `RegionName::new` admits, so a present state is always a name and the
way back to one cannot fail.

ONE WRITER, AS FOR THE REST OF THE GROUP. The mint reads the region the
InitSyn admitted; the InitAck release installs the offer, which holds no
peer's region; the OpenSyn rebuild installs what the cookie carried. The
reopen reset had its own region clear (R2774); that is now a second writer
of a slot `return_to_offer` already writes, so it went, and the reopen
witness is what says the one that remains does the job.

A BEHAVIOUR MOVES, AND THE TESTS THAT PINNED THE OLD ONE MOVED WITH IT. Until
now the acceptor reported the peer's region from the InitSyn on. Upstream
reports it only once the handshake completes -- the region reaches the
transport's config from the state rebuilt out of the cookie. Three tests in
init_region_name.rs read the region at InitAck, which after this round is
precisely the moment the acceptor must hold none. Found by reading every
reader of the slot BEFORE building, not by the tests going red: their
harness now drives the OpenSyn that echoes the acceptor's own cookie and
reads the region once it is admitted. A refused InitSyn gets no InitAck and
so no OpenSyn, so the refusal arms read what they always read.

THE COST IS ON THE MICROBIT'S STACK. The member is fixed-width, so every
cookie carries 33 bytes for it, named or not; the acceptor's deepest frame
grew 40 bytes, and its margin is now 460 of 7168. A variable-width member
would have saved cookie bytes and none of the frame, since the value is
built at full width either way.

THE GRADE STAYS PARTIAL: the multilink key and challenge and the held head
slots remain.
